passages.text: Invention of an oral medication for cardiac Fabry disease caused by RNA mis-splicing

Pathogenic RNA splicing variants have emerged as promising therapeutic targets due to their role in disease while preserving coding sequences. In this study, we developed RECTAS-2.0, a small molecule designed to correct RNA mis-splicing caused by the GLA c.639+919G>A mutation, which leads to the inclusion of a 57-nucleotide poison exon, resulting in later-onset Fabry disease, particularly prevalent in East Asia. RECTAS-2.0 restored normal GLA mRNA splicing and alpha-galactosidase activity in patient-derived B-lymphoblastoid cell lines and induced pluripotent stem cell-derived cardiomyocytes. Furthermore, oral administration of RECTAS-2.0 effectively corrected splicing in a transgenic mouse model, demonstrating its substantial splice-switching activity and safety for clinical application. RECTAS-2.0 demonstrated potential applicability to other genetic disorders that involve similar exon competition. These findings underscore the therapeutic potential of RECTAS-2.0 for Fabry disease and highlight its broader implications for RNA splicing-targeted therapies in genetic disorders.
An oral drug correcting RNA splicing errors offers a potential treatment for Fabry disease and other splicing-related disorders.
INTRODUCTION

Genetic disorders caused by RNA splicing defects have attracted increasing attention. Many pathogenic variants affect splicing without altering coding sequences, leading to mis-splicing events that produce non-functional proteins or reduced gene expression. Since such mutations do not affect coding sequences, targeting RNA mis-splicing presents a major therapeutic advantage: It enables restoration of full gene function by correcting splicing errors without any change in the protein-coding sequences. This makes RNA-based therapies a promising approach for treating these disorders.

A specific example is the later-onset cardiac variant of Fabry disease (FD), caused by the GLA c.639+919G>A mutation, which is particularly prevalent in East Asia, especially Taiwan. FD is an X-linked lysosomal storage disorder caused by mutations in the GLA gene, which encodes alpha-galactosidase A (alpha-GAL), an enzyme essential for breaking down globotriaosylceramide (Gb3) in tissues. While classical FD affects multiple organs, including the kidneys and heart, the GLA c.639+919G>A mutation primarily causes cardiac manifestations with minimal involvement of other organs. This mutation disrupts a splicing silencer, leading to the activation of a 57-nucleotide poison exon, introducing a premature stop codon and triggering mRNA degradation via nonsense-mediated mRNA decay (NMD). Although some properly spliced transcripts remain, producing limited amounts of functional alpha-GAL, the residual enzyme activity, typically around 5% of normal levels, is insufficient to prevent the later-onset cardiac symptoms. This mutation is reported to have spread throughout East and Southeast Asia due to a founder effect originating in China more than 800 years ago. The prevalence of this mutation is particularly high in Taiwan, affecting 1 in 875 males and 1 in 399 females, and it accounts for 82 to 86% of cardiac Fabry cases, representing a serious disease burden in the region.

Current treatments for FD include enzyme replacement therapy (ERT) and pharmacological chaperones. ERT consists of biweekly intravenous infusion of recombinant alpha-GAL to replace the deficient enzyme, while pharmacological chaperones bind to and stabilize misfolded, partially active mutant alpha-GALs to enhance their function. Although ERT is beneficial to patients, it requires lifelong biweekly infusions, thus making it invasive and costly. Pharmacological chaperones, on the other hand, are not applicable to this specific mutation. In light of these limitations, there is an urgent need for novel therapies that specifically target RNA mis-splicing, potentially offering a more effective, less invasive treatment option.

We previously reported splice-switching small molecules as a new modality targeting pathogenic splicing defects and demonstrated their effects for DMD gene mis-splicing in Duchenne muscular dystrophy, IKBKG gene mis-splicing in NEMO deficiency syndrome, CFTR gene mis-splicing in cystic fibrosis, and IKBKAP gene mis-splicing in familial dysautonomia. Since our compounds modulate splicing patterns by biasing the strength of exon recognition between competing exons, it may also be applicable to other genetic disorders caused by similar splicing defects arising from abnormal exon competition. In this study, we investigated the mechanism of poison exon recognition caused by the GLA c.639+919G>A mutation and evaluated whether our compounds could correct the splicing defects and enzyme deficiency, aiming to develop a clinically viable, orally available treatment for FD. To investigate this, we evaluated the ability of our compound to restore normal splicing and improve alpha-GAL enzyme activity, using patient-derived cells and a transgenic mouse model.
RESULTS
RECTAS suppresses GLA poison exon in patient B-LCLs

The GLA c.639+919G>A mutation activates a 57-nucleotide poison exon within the GLA gene, leading to the introduction of a premature stop codon and subsequent NMD, reducing functional alpha-GAL proteins (Fig. 1A). To assess whether the c.639+919 G>A-dependent GLA poison exon can be controlled by our splice-switching compounds, we prepared B-lymphoblastoid cell lines (B-LCLs) from patients with FD with the c.639+919 G>A GLA mutation, as well as those from healthy volunteers. We tested the splice-switching potential of several small-molecule compounds that we and others have reported, including CDC-like kinase (CLK) activator RECTAS, CLK inhibitors TG003 and TG693, serine-arginine protein kinase inhibitor SRPIN340, and SF3B1 inhibitor FR901464. Reverse transcriptase polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) analysis demonstrated that RECTAS significantly reduced the inclusion of the poison exon in a dose-dependent manner in two FD patient-derived B-LCL strains (Fig. 1B), suggesting its potent splice-switching activity. No effect on GLA splicing or expression was observed in control B-LCLs (Fig. 1C). Furthermore, RECTAS treatment restored alpha-GAL enzyme activity in FD patient-derived B-LCLs in a dose-dependent manner (Fig. 1D), underscoring its potential to correct the splicing defect and restore enzyme function.
RECTAS suppresses the pathogenic GLA poison exon inclusion caused by the c.639+919G>A mutation.

RECTAS reduces Gb3 accumulation in patient iPSC-CMs

Given the effectiveness of RECTAS in suppressing the GLA poison exon in B-LCLs, we next investigated whether this splice-switching effect could be reproduced in cardiomyocytes, the primary tissue affected by this mutation. To this end, we established induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) from female patients with FD and differentiated them into cardiomyocytes (iPSC-CMs). Because of X-chromosome inactivation, iPSCs derived from female patients express either the wild-type (wt) or mutated (mut) X chromosome. As a result, we were able to establish both wt allele-activated iPSCs (iPSCs/wt) as controls and mut allele-activated iPSCs (iPSCs/mut) as disease models from the same patient.

Cardiomyocytes derived from iPSCs/mut (iPSC-CMs/mut) exhibited marked accumulation of Gb3 in lysosomes (Fig. 1, E, bottom, and F), consistent with FD pathology, whereas iPSC-CMs/wt showed no such accumulation (Fig. 1E, top). Upon differentiation, iPSC-CMs/mut predominantly expressed GLA transcripts containing the poison exon, but treatment with RECTAS (30 muM, 72 hours) restored normal splicing (Fig. 1G). This correction at the mRNA level was reflected at the protein level, with a significant increase in alpha-GAL protein (Fig. 1H). RECTAS-treated iPSC-CMs/mut demonstrated a 2.69-fold increase in alpha-GAL protein [95% confidence interval (CI): 1.98- to 3.39-fold], leading to a 15.7% reduction in Gb3 accumulation (95% CI: 6.4 to 25.1%) (Fig. 1I). These results confirm that RECTAS restores functional alpha-GAL expression and reduces pathological Gb3 accumulation in FD-relevant cells.

In addition, we evaluated the transcriptome-wide effects of RECTAS in iPSC-CMs/mut. As previously reported for human fibroblasts, RECTAS had minimal impact on overall RNA splicing, affecting only 0.23% of total splicing events with a false discovery rate (FDR) < 0.05 (Fig. 1, J and K). Among all alternative splicing (AS) events, the exon skipping rate of the c.639+919 G>A-induced GLA poison exon was in the top 29%, demonstrating RECTAS's high selectivity for this target (Fig. 1L and data S1).
SRSF6 suppresses GLA poison exon inclusion

We next investigated the mechanism by which RECTAS modulates the skipping of the GLA poison exon caused by the c.639+919 G>A mutation. To this end, we used a SPREADD reporter system, a dual-fluorescence splicing reporter designed for precise quantification. In this system, the skipping or inclusion of the poison exon is reflected by the expression of green fluorescent protein (GFP) or red fluorescent protein (RFP), respectively, allowing for the measurement of relative splicing events by analyzing the GFP/RFP ratio in HeLa cells (Fig. 2A). RECTAS treatment dose-dependently restored normal splicing of GLA in this reporter system (Fig. 2, B and C). In contrast, kinetin, a plant cytokinin structurally related to RECTAS, showed no effect on GLA splicing (Fig. 2, B and C), which is consistent with our previous findings that kinetin exhibits much weaker splice-switching activity for mis-splicing caused by the IKBKAP IVS20+6T>C mutation compared to RECTAS.
RECTAS prevents poison exon inclusion by promoting SRSF6-dependent exon 5 recognition in GLA.

Representative fluorescent images (B) and quantification plot (C). (D) RNA oligonucleotide sequences for the pulldown assay. SRSF6 binding sites predicted by ESE Finder are highlighted for E5_#2. (E) Western blot of pulldown assay shows SRSF6 binding to E5_#2. (F) RECTAS effects on GLA splicing examined with or without siRNA knockdown of SRSF6/SRSF8. (G and H) Effects of SRSF6 binding site mutations on RECTAS-induced exon skipping. (I and J) In vitro splicing assay for GLA exon 4 and poison exon. Pre-mRNA constructs (I) and splicing results (J). We have previously demonstrated that the splice-switching activity of RECTAS is mediated through its interaction with the splicing factor SRSF6, which regulates the correction of IKBKAP mis-splicing. We therefore hypothesized that SRSF6 also plays a critical role in modulating the GLA poison exon. To test this hypothesis, we performed RNA pulldown assays and identified strong binding of SRSF6 to a region downstream of exon 5 (Fig. 2, D and E, E5_#2). Computational analysis using ESE Finder 3.0 revealed the presence of high-affinity SRSF6 binding motifs within this region (Fig. 2D). Moreover, siRNA-mediated knockdown of SRSF6, but not of other splicing factors such as SRSF8, resulted in a marked reduction of RECTAS-induced exon skipping, underscoring the critical role of SRSF6 in mediating GLA splicing correction (Fig. 2F). Deletion and point mutation of the SRSF6 binding sites resulted in reduced RECTAS activity, further supporting the key role of SRSF6 in mediating the splicing correction (Fig. 2, G and H).
RECTAS promotes exon 5 selection over the poison exon

We next investigated how SRSF6 promotes RECTAS-induced skipping of the GLA poison exon. In general, splicing activators like SRSF6 adjust the recognition of suboptimal, or "weak," splice sites by recruiting U1snRNP and U2snRNP. This mechanism is especially important when two competing exons are both suboptimal, as splicing factors can bias the selection toward one exon over the other. In the case of GLA, the splice donor site (SD) of exon 4 is first recognized by U1snRNP cotranscriptionally, initiating the splicing process. Subsequently, a decision is made between the two competing splice acceptor sites (SA) of the poison exon and of exon 5. We hypothesized that SRSF6 binding E5_#2 promotes exon 5 selection over the poison exon by enhancing U2snRNP recruitment to exon 5 SA.

Upon analyzing the splice sites of both exons, we found that exon 5 harbors a weak SA motif, with a poorly conserved branch point sequence (BS) that lacks a consensus yUnAy motif, and a pyrimidine nucleotide at the +1 position. On the other hand, the poison exon has a weak SD that fails to pair efficiently with U1snRNA, contributing to suboptimal SD recognition. Since the U1snRNP-mediated exon definition usually promotes the recognition of upstream SAs within approximately 500 nucleotides, we hypothesized that the weak SD of the poison exon makes its SA suboptimal.

To test this, we used an in vitro splicing assay with pre-mRNA constructs that included exon 4 and the poison exon, with or without compensation for U1 pairing at the -1 position (Fig. 2I). The splicing reaction occurred only with the optimal U1 pairing (optU1) (Fig. 2J, lanes 8 to 13), but not in the absence of U1 compensation (Fig. 2J, lanes 2 to 7), confirming that the SA of the poison exon is suboptimal due to the lack of U1-primed exon definition.

We further confirmed the suboptimal nature of exon 5's SA through a mutation study. By replacing the SA of exon 5 with that of the poison exon (optSA) or substituting both the BS and SA with the corresponding sequences from the poison exon (optBS/SA) (Fig. 2K), we found that optSA enhanced RECTAS-induced normal splicing of GLA, with an even greater effect observed for optBS/SA (Fig. 2L).

These results indicate that there is a competitive selection between two suboptimal exons, the poison exon and exon 5, for splicing of the GLA gene with the c.639+919 G>A mutation (fig. S1). RECTAS enhances the activity of SRSF6, which binds downstream of the exon 5 SA, thereby promoting the selection of exon 5 over the poison exon and favoring the skipping of the poison exon.
Synthesis of RECTAS derivatives

Our observations demonstrated that RECTAS effectively suppresses the pathogenic GLA poison exon. However, a RECTAS dose of 10 muM or higher was required to achieve this effect. Given that the plasma concentration of RECTAS was limited to 6 to 8 muM in mice administered RECTAS per os (p.o.) at 100 mg/kg body weight (mg/kg-BW), it was evident that improving the pharmaceutical efficacy was necessary for therapeutic application. To address this, we aimed to isolate RECTAS derivatives with enhanced splice-switching activity against the c.639+919 G>A mutation-induced GLA poison exon, using the SPREADD reporter system for quantifying splicing events based on GFP/RFP dual fluorescence (Fig. 3A).
Identification of RECTAS-2.0 through phenotypic screening for GLA (c.639+919G>A) splicing correction.

Since commercially available RECTAS analogs were limited and none showed sufficient splice-switching activity for GLA (table S1), we synthesized 418 RECTAS derivatives and screened them for poison exon-skipping efficiency based on GFP/RFP fluorescence intensities. Of the 418 compounds, 248 (59.3%) demonstrated superior splice-switching activity compared to RECTAS, and seven compounds exhibited over fivefold greater activity than RECTAS (Fig. 3B and data S2). Taking into account factors such as in vitro stability, oral bioavailability, and scalability, we selected cpd5819 (Fig. 3C), hereafter referred to as "RECTAS-2.0," for further characterization.

RECTAS-2.0 exhibited approximately 10-fold higher potency (1 muM RECTAS-2.0 versus 10 muM RECTAS) and over fivefold greater efficacy (10 muM RECTAS-2.0 versus 10 muM RECTAS) in correcting c.639+919G>A-induced GLA splicing (Fig. 3D). In addition, RECTAS-2.0 was more efficiently absorbed into the bloodstream and delivered to heart tissue compared to other RECTAS derivatives (Kp value of 0.75 and plasma concentration of ~75%) (Fig. 3F and tables S2 and S3). Given that cardiac symptoms are the sole manifestation in patients with FD harboring the c.639+919 G>A mutation, the efficient delivery of RECTAS-2.0 to heart tissue is particularly advantageous for treating this cardiac variant of FD.
RECTAS-2.0 is more effective in iPSC-CMs

We next evaluated the therapeutic effect of RECTAS-2.0 in FD patient-derived iPSC-CMs. Consistent with the restoration of normal GLA splicing observed in the SPREADD reporter assay (Fig. 3D), treatment with RECTAS-2.0 more effectively suppressed GLA poison exon inclusion and increased overall GLA gene expression in iPSC-CMs/mut compared to RECTAS (Fig. 4, A and B). The recovery of alpha-GAL protein and enzyme activity were also significantly higher with RECTAS-2.0 than with RECTAS (Fig. 4, C and D). Furthermore, Gb3 accumulation in iPSC-CMs/mut decreased by 31.8% (95% CI: 24.9 to 38.7%) following RECTAS-2.0 treatment (Fig. 4E). These results provide further evidence that RECTAS-2.0 can rescue GLA expression in iPSC-CMs derived from patients with FD by effectively inhibiting poison exon recognition caused by the c.639+919G>A splicing mutation.
RECTAS-2.0 exhibits therapeutic effects in FD models with the c.639+919 G>A splicing mutation.

RECTAS-2.0 skips poison exon in Tg mouse hearts

Following the successful demonstration of the therapeutic potential of RECTAS-2.0 in vitro using FD patient-derived iPSC-CMs (Fig. 4, A to E), we next investigated whether RECTAS-2.0 could be effectively delivered to cardiomyocytes to correct c.639+919 G>A-induced GLA mis-splicing in vivo. Given that no existing animal model mimics the GLA poison exon mis-splicing, we generated a transgenic mouse model by introducing the human GLA gene carrying the c.639+919 G>A-mutated intron 4 (Fig. 4F), which we termed Tg(GLA:c.639+919G>A). This transgene is expected to be degraded by NMD, as seen in GLA transcripts from patients with FD with this mutation. We confirmed NMD-mediated degradation of the poison exon-containing GLA mRNA using peripheral blood cells isolated from Tg(GLA:c.639+919G>A) mice, treated with the NMD inhibitor cycloheximide (CHX) (Fig. 4G). Although the Tg(GLA:c.639+919G>A) mice retain the endogenous murine Gla gene (Fig. 4G), precluding analysis of disease-related phenotypes such as alpha-GAL enzyme activity and Gb3 accumulation, this model remains useful for evaluating drug delivery and splicing modulation efficacy in cardiomyocytes in vivo.

We next administered RECTAS or RECTAS-2.0 orally (p.o.) to assess their splice-switching efficacy in vivo (Fig. 4H). Tg(GLA:c.639+919G>A) mice received either vehicle (0.5% MC), RECTAS (100 mg/kg-BW), or RECTAS-2.0 (30 or 100 mg/kg-BW) twice at 3-hour intervals. Six hours after the first administration, heart tissues were analyzed for the expression of GLA mRNA. We specifically quantified mRNA exhibiting normal splicing between exon 4 and exon 5, as the poison exon-containing transcripts are largely degraded via NMD (Fig. 4G). In heart tissues from Tg mice treated with RECTAS (100 mg/kg-BW), we observed an approximate 20% restoration of functional GLA mRNA levels compared to vehicle-treated controls (Fig. 4I). Notably, RECTAS-2.0 demonstrated enhanced efficacy, with ~30% restoration at 30 mg/kg-BW and ~40% at 100 mg/kg-BW (Fig. 4J). This superior performance of RECTAS-2.0 compared to RECTAS aligns with the in vitro results, further validating the model of small molecule-mediated splice-switching to improve functional GLA expression (Fig. 4K).

Considering the potential clinical application of RECTAS-2.0, we evaluated its safety profile across various tests. In rats, no adverse effects were observed following single-doses p.o. administration of RECTAS-2.0 at 0, 100, 300, and 1,000 mg/kg-BW, suggesting that RECTAS-2.0 is well-tolerated (table S4). Furthermore, RECTAS-2.0 demonstrated no mutagenic effects in the Ames test (table S5) and did not impair ex vivo heart function in the rabbit Langendorff heart test (table S6). RECTAS-2.0 also showed no significant impact on hERG channel inhibition (table S7). Collectively, these results indicate that RECTAS-2.0 is nongenotoxic and does not induce acute adverse effects on cardiac function.
DISCUSSION

In this study, we demonstrated that RECTAS, one of our splicing modulators, effectively suppressed the pathogenic poison exon inclusion caused by the GLA c.639+919G>A mutation in both B-LCLs and iPSC-CMs derived from patients with FD. Through synthetic optimization, we developed RECTAS-2.0, a novel splice-switching compound with markedly enhanced efficacy for rescuing GLA expression both in vitro and in vivo.

FD, caused by alpha-GAL deficiency, is a multisystemic lysosomal storage disorder. When alpha-GAL enzyme activity falls below 1% of normal levels, the severe, classical form of FD develops, primarily affecting the heart, kidneys, and nervous system. In contrast, residual enzyme activity of 5 to 10% is associated with a later-onset cardiac variant. Patients with this cardiac variant of FD typically develop left ventricular hypertrophy and arrhythmias in early adulthood, although the accumulation of Gb3 in heart tissue begins before clinical symptoms appear. Newborn screening in Taiwan has revealed an unexpectedly high incidence of the GLA c.639+919G>A mutation, which is prevalent throughout East Asia due to a founder effect. Individuals with this mutation exhibit a wide range of disease onset, from early adulthood to remaining asymptomatic for life; however, the development of cardiac symptoms can often be life-threatening. Early detection and intervention are crucial for preserving quality of life and mitigating the serious disease burden associated with this mutation in the region.

Currently, recombinant alpha-GAL enzymes, such as agalsidase alpha and agalsidase beta, are widely used as ERT for the treatment of FD. ERT is currently regarded as the most effective treatment for FD, in particular for systemic involvement; however, it presents limitations, especially in treating cardiac manifestations. For example, in heart biopsies from two male patients after several months of ERT, Gb3 deposits persisted in cardiomyocytes and smooth muscles, despite clearance in endothelial cells. In addition, the repeated infusions necessary for ERT increase the risk of developing antibodies against the exogenous enzyme, which can reduce its long-term efficacy. The high cost of ERT poses a substantial financial burden as a preemptive treatment in Taiwan, where the GLA c.639+919G>A mutation is prevalent. In addition, the biweekly infusion regimen required for ERT is logistically challenging, making long-term adherence difficult for patients, in particular those in the workforce. On the other hand, migalastat, a pharmacological chaperone, offers an alternative, orally available treatment for FD. However, its effectiveness is limited to specific "migalastat-amenable" missense mutations that result in unstable but functionally recoverable alpha-GAL. Since the c.639+919G>A mutation is not a missense mutation, it falls outside the migalastat treatment eligibility.

On the basis of the migalastat-amenability criteria used in clinical practice, which assess therapeutic efficacy based on alpha-GAL activity, we extrapolated these benchmarks to evaluate the clinical potential of RECTAS and RECTAS-2.0. The migalastat-amenability assay, a good laboratory practice-validated test conducted in human embryonic kidney (HEK) 293 cells, defines amenable mutations as those achieving a >=1.20-fold increase in alpha-GAL activity above baseline, with an absolute increase of >=3.0% of wt alpha-GAL activity when treated with 10 muM migalastat. In our study, RECTAS and RECTAS-2.0 demonstrated markedly higher increases in alpha-GAL activity in iPSC-CMs derived from patients with FD carrying the c.639+919G>A mutation. Treatment with RECTAS at 10 muM resulted in a 1.43-fold increase in alpha-GAL activity, while RECTAS-2.0 achieved fold increases of 1.47 at 1 muM and 1.87 at 10 muM. The absolute increases in enzyme activity were 8.5, 9.2, and 17.2% relative to wt iPSC-CMs, respectively. Despite differences in assay methodologies, both assays assess the increase in alpha-GAL activity as a key measure of therapeutic efficacy. These values far surpass the thresholds defined in the migalastat-amenability test, highlighting the superior clinical potential of RECTAS and RECTAS-2.0 for treating patients with FD with the c.639+919G>A mutation.

For the correction of aberrant RNA splicing caused by c.639+919G>A mutation, several approaches were reported. Antisense oligonucleotides (AONs) targeting U1snRNP have been explored as a therapeutic approach to splice-switching, in particular through the use of a minigene system to promote poison exon skipping in transfected COS-1 cells. Although AONs have demonstrated efficacy in correcting aberrant splicing events caused by cryptic splice site activation in various genetic disorders, such as Duchenne muscular dystrophy and retinal dystrophies, they face considerable limitations in clinical applications. Specifically, AONs exhibit poor tissue penetration and reduced metabolic stability, even when administered intravenously. Moreover, oral administration of AONs is ineffective, making them less attractive as a long-term therapeutic option, in particular for young adults diagnosed to have this GLA mutation. There is also a study investigating the potential of amiloride, a well-known diuretic, to suppress abnormal splicing associated with the GLA c.639+919G>A mutation. By interfering with the spliceosome complex, amiloride successfully promoted poison exon skipping in B-LCLs, presenting a more patient-friendly oral alternative. While these findings are promising, the concentrations of amiloride used in the study were relatively high. Further investigation is required to determine its therapeutic potential in real-world settings.

Over the past decade, the critical role of splicing defects in genetic diseases has become increasingly apparent. In this report, we demonstrated that our splice-switching compound, RECTAS, exerts its therapeutic effects by specifically enhancing the recognition strength of correct exons in cases where two suboptimal exons are competing. RECTAS modulates splicing patterns through the activation of SRSF6, which strengthens the recognition of specific suboptimal exons. When SRSF6 enhances the recognition of the authentic exon, RECTAS is able to restore aberrant splicing patterns, as evidenced by its effects on both GLA and IKBKAP mutations. This mechanism suggests that RECTAS has broader applicability to other genetic disorders caused by competition between suboptimal exons, where proper exon recognition can be facilitated through the modulation of SRSF6.

Rather than targeting the disease pathology directly, our compound addresses the underlying genetic defect responsible for disease development. If clinical trials in diseases with larger patient populations, such as FD or familial dysautonomia, confirm safety and efficacy, RECTAS could potentially be applied to other conditions involving suboptimal exon competition, even in cases where the patient population is too small for feasible clinical trials. This approach could extend the therapeutic use of RECTAS to rare genetic disorders characterized by competitive exon recognition, offering a novel strategy for treating otherwise difficult-to-manage conditions.

In conclusion, we demonstrated that RECTAS and its derivative, RECTAS-2.0, successfully corrected the pathogenic GLA mis-splicing caused by the c.639+919G>A mutation in cardiac patients with FD. Although additional preclinical studies are required to thoroughly evaluate off-target effects and species-specific differences in RNA splicing regulation before advancing to clinical trials, our preclinical data thus far have revealed no notable adverse effects. This positions RECTAS-2.0 as a promising candidate for the preemptive oral treatment of cardiac FD, offering a novel therapeutic approach in particular for patients with limited existing treatment options.
MATERIALS AND METHODS
Cell lines

HeLa cells were obtained from the Japanese Collection of Research Bioresources Cell Bank of the National Institutes of Biomedical Innovation, Health and Nutrition (Osaka, Japan), and cultured in Dulbecco's modified Eagle's medium (Nacalai Tesque, Kyoto, Japan) supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum and antibiotics [penicillin (100 U/ml) and streptomycin (100 mug/ml)] (Nacalai Tesque) in a cell incubator at 37 C, 5% CO2, and 85 to 95% relative humidity. Immortalization of patient B cells was conducted through the infection of culture supernatant of B95.8 to PBMCs obtained from patients with FD with the c.639+919G>A mutation of the GLA gene and healthy donors. The established B-LCLs were cultured in RPMI-1640 medium (Biological Industries, Kibbutz Beit-Haemek, Israel) supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA), 1% l-glutamine, 1% nonessential amino acids, 1% sodium pyruvate (Biological Industries) in a cell incubator at 37 C, 5% CO2, and 85 to 95% relative humidity. The preparation and experiments of B-LCLs were conducted under the approval of the ethics committees of Taipei Veterans General Hospital (2015-04-010C#2) and Kyoto University Graduate School of Medicine (R0091, G259), respectively, with written informed consent obtained from all participants. iPSCs were developed from peripheral blood mononuclear cells of two female donors, through episomal overexpression of OCT3/4, SOX2, KLF4, L-MYC, LIN28, EBNA1, and mp53-DD. FD is an X-linked disease, and in female cell lines, either the wt or the mut X chromosome is activated in each clone. Thus, we used pairs of wt and mut iPSCs from the same donor to minimize differences in genetic background. iPSCs were maintained in mTeSR1 medium (STEMCELL Technologies, Vancouver, Canada) on Matrigel (Corning, Corning, NY, USA) and then differentiated into cardiomyocytes using the PSC Cardiomyocyte Differentiation Kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific) following the manufacturer's protocol. iPSC-CMs were dissociated using Accutase (Innovative Cell Technologies, San Diego, CA, USA), reseeded on Matrigel-coated plates on day 11 of differentiation, and used for downstream assays 3 days later. All of the experiments were conducted three or five times on different days with different batches of iPSC-CMs. The establishment and use of iPSCs were approved by the institutional ethics committee of Kyoto University Graduate School of Medicine (R0091, G259). All the materials are available upon request within the range of the ethical approval.
Compounds

RECTAS [2-chloro-N-(furan-2-ylmethyl)-7H-purin-6-amine, C10H8ClN5O, molecular weight = 249.66] was synthesized as previously described. RECTAS-2.0 [I-5-(((2-chloro-4-((furan-2-ylmethyl)amino)-1,7-naphthyridin-8-yl)oxy)methyl)-3-methyloxazolidin-2-one, C18H17ClN4O4, molecular weight = 388.81] was synthesized by the following sequential reactions: (i) 8-Methoxy-2H-pyrido[3,4-d][1,3]oxazine-2,4(1H)-dione was obtained by adding triphosgene (5.84 mmol) to a suspension of 3-amino-2-methoxyisonicotinic acid (1, 5.96 mmol) in tetrahydrofuran (THF) and stirring overnight at room temperature. The mixture was concentrated under reduced pressure and Et2O was added to the residue. The resulting precipitate was collected by filtration. (ii) To a mixture of sodium hydride (7.30 mmol) in N,N-dimethylformamide (DMF) was added 8-methoxy-2H-pyrido[3,4-d][1,3]oxazine-2,4(1H)-dione (5.61 mmol) and diethyl malonate (56.0 mmol) in DMF and stirred at 160 C for 4 hours. Then, 1 M HCl was added to acidify the reaction solution, followed by extraction with ethyl acetate. The organic layer was washed with brine, dried over anhydrous sodium sulfate, and concentrated under reduced pressure. Et2O was added to the obtained residue, and the resulting precipitate was collected by filtration to obtain 4-hydroxy-8-methoxy-2-oxo-1,2-dihydro-1,7-naphthyridine-3-carboxylate. (iii) A mixture of ethyl 4-hydroxy-8-methoxy-2-oxo-1,2-dihydro-1,7-naphthyridine-3-carboxylate (3.41 mmol) and potassium hydroxide (12.7 mmol) in H2O was stirred at 120 C for 16 hours. Then, 1 M HCl was added to acidify the reaction mixture, followed by stirring at 0 C for 0.5 hours. The resulting precipitate was collected by filtration to obtain 4-hydroxy-8-methoxy-1,7-naphthyridin-2(1H)-one. (iv) N-phenylbis(trifluoromethanesulfonimide) (1.24 mmol) was added to a THF solution of 4-hydroxy-8-methoxy-1,7-naphthyridin-2(1H)-one (1.04 mmol) and triethylamine (3.11 mmol) and stirred overnight at room temperature. The reaction mixture was concentrated under reduced pressure, CHCl3 was added to the obtained residue, and the resulting precipitate was collected by filtration. The filtrate was concentrated under reduced pressure, and the resulting residue was purified by silica gel column chromatography (ethyl acetate/n-hexane = 25/75 to 50/50) to obtain 8-methoxy-2-oxo-1,2-dihydro-1,7-naphthyridin-4-yl trifluoromethanesulfonate. (v) Furfurylamine (8.86 mmol) was added to an acetonitrile suspension of 8-methoxy-2-oxo-1,2-dihydro-1,7-naphthyridin-4-yl trifluoromethanesulfonate (2.95 mmol) and stirred at 60 C for 6 hours. After allowing the reaction mixture to cool to room temperature, it was concentrated under reduced pressure until the solution volume was decreased by about half, and the resulting solid was collected by filtration. The obtained crude product was washed with ice-cooled acetonitrile to obtain 4-[(furan-2-ylmethyl)amino]-8-methoxy-1,7-naphthyridin-2(1H)-one. (vi) To a mixture of 4-[(furan-2-ylmethyl)amino]-8-methoxy-1,7-naphthyridin-2(1H)-one (1.98 mmol) and phosphoryl chloride (109 mmol) was added N,N-diethylaniline (3.96 mmol), and the mixture was stirred at 90 C for 3 hours and then stirred at 100 C for 9 hours. After allowing the reaction mixture to cool to room temperature, it was concentrated under reduced pressure. Chloroform was added to the resulting residue, and a saturated aqueous sodium hydrogen carbonate solution was added to neutralize the mixture with vigorous stirring, followed by extraction with chloroform and concentration under reduced pressure. The resulting residue was purified by amino silica gel column chromatography (ethyl acetate/n-hexane = 0/100 to 40/60) to obtain 2,8-dichloro-N-(furan-2-ylmethyl)-1,7-naphthyridin-4-amine. (vii) To an acetonitrile solution (7.2 ml) of 2,8-dichloro-N-(furan-2-ylmethyl)-1,7-naphthyridin-4-amine (0.714 mmol) was added (5R)-5-(hydroxymethyl)-3-methyl-1,3-oxazolidin-2-one (0.928 mmol) and cesium carbonate (1.45 mmol) and treated with a microwave reactor at 110 C for 2.5 hours. After allowing the reaction mixture to cool to room temperature, ethyl acetate was added and insoluble matter was filtered, and the filtrate was then concentrated under reduced pressure. The obtained residue was purified by amino silica gel column chromatography (ethyl acetate/n-hexane = 20/80 to 100/0) to obtain (5R)-5-[({2-chloro-4-[(furan-2-ylmethyl)amino]-1,7-naphthyridin-8-yl}oxy)methyl]-3-methyl-1,3-oxazolidin-2-one (RECTAS-2.0).
RT-PCR and qPCR

Total RNA was collected from cell lines using Direct-zol RNA Miniprep Kit (Zymo Research, Irvine, CA, USA). For total RNA extraction from heart tissues, 5- to 8-mm heart tissue blocks were minced and incubated in TRIzol reagent (Thermo Fisher Scientific). After homogenization, total RNA was purified using Direct-zol RNA Miniprep Kit (Zymo Research). cDNA was synthesized using Prime Star reverse transcriptase (Takara Bio, Kusatsu, Japan) with a random hexamer for cell line samples, and High-Capacity RNA-to-cDNA kit (Themo Fisher Scientific) for mouse heart tissue samples. PCR was then conducted using Ex Taq DNA polymerase (Takara Bio) for cell lines, and AmpliTaq Gold 360 (Thermo Fisher Scientific) for mouse heart tissue samples. The primer sets used in the RT-PCR are listed in data S3. For quantification of overall GLA expression, the relative quantity of GLA expression compared to glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase (GAPDH) as an internal control was measured using TaqMan probes targeting GLA exons 2 and 3 (Hs00609238_m1) and GAPDH (Hs99999905_m1). GLA expression levels were first normalized to GAPDH and then to the mean expression levels of dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO)-treated wt samples.
Western blotting

For Western blotting, cell lysates were dissolved in Laemmli buffer and subjected to 5 to 15% polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis (PAGE); the gels were then electro-transferred to a polyvinylidene fluoride membrane. These transferred membranes were then incubated with 5% skim milk for 1 hour at room temperature and washed three times for 15 min each with phosphate-buffered saline (PBS), followed by incubation with primary antibodies dissolved in PBS overnight at 4 C. Membranes were then washed with PBS + 0.1% Tween 20 (PBST) three times for 15 min each, and incubated with secondary antibody diluted in PBS with 1% skim milk for 60 min at room temperature. Membranes were subsequently washed with PBST three times for 15 min each, and chemiluminescence signals were obtained using SuperSignal West Pico substrate (Thermo Fisher Scientific) or Femto Maximum Sensitivity substrate (Thermo Fisher Scientific). The signals were captured using the ChemiDoc Touch MP Imaging system (Bio-Rad, Hercules, CA, USA). The following antibodies were used as primary antibody in this study: anti-phospho-SRSFs mouse monoclonal antibody (1H4G7, #33-9400) (Thermo Fisher Scientific) and anti-alpha-GAL rabbit monoclonal antibody (Abcam, Cambridge, UK). For the secondary antibody, horseradish peroxidase (HRP)-conjugated goat anti-mouse IgG polyclonal antibody (Abcam) was used. For the detection of endogenous GAPDH, HRP-conjugated mouse anti-GAPDH antibody (OriGene, Rockville, MD, USA) was used.
In vitro splicing assay

For the in vitro splicing assay, pre-mRNA substrates were synthesized by in vitro transcription using the T7 in vitro system (Takara Bio). 5'-RNA capping was conducted using 10 mM m7G(5')ppp(5') in the presence of 1 mM guanosine 5'-triphosphate, 10 mM adenosine 5'-triphosphate (ATP), 10 mM uridine 5'-triphosphate, 1 mM guanosine 5'-triphosphate, alpha-32P cytidine 5'-triphosphate, and 100 mM dithiothreitol during in vitro transcription at 37 C for 2 hours. DNA templates for in vitro transcription were prepared by overlapping PCR: the fragment with oAM39+oAM44 was annealed with that of oAM40+oAM45 (E4+Psi), oAM40+oAM47 (E4+Psi, optU1), oAM40+oAM46 (E4+Psi, G>A), and oAM40+oAM48 (E4+Psi, G>A and optU1), and further amplified by PCR with oAM39+oAM45 (E4+Psi), oAM39+oAM47 (E4+Psi, optU1), oAM39+oAM46 (E4+Psi, G>A), and oAM39+oAM49 (E4+Psi, G>A and optU1). The resulting pre-mRNA constructs consisted of the GLA exon 4 through the poison exon [nucleotide positions 7257 to 8280, according to NG_007119 of National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI)] with partial truncation of intron 4 (nucleotide positions 7449 to 7997). The primer sequences used for pre-mRNA template synthesis are presented in data S3. alpha-32P-labeled pre-mRNA substrates were then gel-purified from 6% PAGE gel with 7.5 M urea. Next, an in vitro splicing assay was conducted using 4 ng of 32P-labeled purified pre-mRNAs, in the presence of 0.5 or 3 mM MgCl2, RNase inhibitor (Promega, Madison, WI, USA), splicing nuclear extract (CILBIOTECH, S.A., Mons, Belgium), and splicing reaction buffer [0.6% polyvinyl alcohol, 0.4 mM ATP, 20 mM creatine phosphate, and 5 mM HEPES (pH 7.9)] at 30 C for 2 hours. The splicing reaction was terminated by adding stop solution [30 mM tris-HCl (pH 7.4), 30 mM sodium acetate, 0.5% SDS, 2 mM EDTA, and yeast total RNA (3 mug/ml) as carrier RNA]. Reaction products were mixed with loading dye (98% formamide, 10 mM EDTA, 0.1% xylene cyanol, and 0.1% bromophenol blue) and separated in 6% PAGE gel with 7.5 M urea, along with a 100-base pair ladder (Thermo Fisher Scientific), labeled with alpha-32P ATP. 32P signals were then captured using BAS-MS Imaging Plates (Fujifilm, Tokyo, Japan) and visualized with Typhoon FLA 9500 (GE Healthcare, Chicago, IL, USA).
RNA pulldown assay

HeLa cell lysates were prepared using lysis buffer (10 mM tris-HCl, pH 7.4), 150 mM NaCl, 1 mM ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid, 1% Triton X-100, 0.1% sodium dodecyl sulfate, 0.25% sodium deoxycholate, and 10% glycerol with protease inhibitor (Nacalai Tesque) and phosphatase inhibitor (Sigma-Aldrich, St. Louis, MO, USA), followed by flush sonication and treatment with deoxyribonuclease I (Promega) at 37 C for 5 min. Supernatants were then collected by centrifugation (14,000 rpm at 4 C for 15 min) and incubated with 5'-biotin, 3'-dTdT-attached RNA oligos for 16 hours with rotation at 4 C, followed by washing with tris-buffered saline three times and elution with Laemmli buffer. Samples rotated without bait RNA oligo served as a negative control. Eluted proteins were then analyzed by Western blotting.
Dual-fluorescence splicing reporter assay

The SPREADD splicing reporter system was applied for GLA poison exon splicing induced by the c.639+919G>A mutation, and relative rates of normally spliced GLA exons 4 and 5 were quantified using the ratio of GFP to RFP. For the splicing reporter assay, the GLA exons 4 to 5-containing construct was transfected into HeLa cells (0.1 x 106 cells per well, seeded in a 12-well plate) with Lipofectamine 2000 transfection reagent (Thermo Fisher Scientific), with replacement with fresh medium 5 hours after the transfection. Subsequently, cells were further incubated with or without compounds for 18 hours before fixation with 4% paraformaldehyde in PBS (pH 7.4). The fixed cells were then scanned with a BZ-X710 fluorescence microscope (Keyence, Osaka, Japan) and analyzed for fluorescence intensity with a BZ-X analyzer and hybrid cell count software (Keyence). The resulting GFP/RFP fluorescence ratio was then plotted.
siRNA knockdown assay

Knockdown was conducted by the lipofection of small interfering RNA (siRNA) (Silencer Select siRNA, Ambion of Thermo Fisher Scientific) for human SRSF6 (siRNA ID, s12741), SRSF8 (siRNA ID, s21495), or a nonspecific control (si-NS) (siRNA ID, 4390843) into HeLa cells using Lipofectamine RNAiMAX (Thermo Fisher Scientific). The final concentration of each siRNA in the culture medium was set to 40 nM. Forty-eight hours after the transfection, cells were transfected with GLA poison exon SPREADD reporter using Lipofectamine 2000 (Thermo Fisher Scientific) for 5 hours. Culture media were then refreshed and further incubated with or without 10 muM RECTAS for 18 hours. GFP/RFP ratios were then quantified as mentioned above.
GLA enzyme activity assay

Fluorometric enzymatic assay of alpha-GAL was performed as described previously with minor modification. alpha-GAL activity was determined by incubating aliquots of the cell lysate at 37 C for 2 hours with 5 mM 4-methylumbelliferyl-alpha-d-galactopyranoside (Sigma-Aldrich) in citrate/phosphate buffer, pH 4.6, in the presence of 0.1 M N-acetylgalactosamine (Sigma-Aldrich), a specific inhibitor of N-acetylgalactosaminidase. The enzymatic cleavage liberated the fluorochrome from 4-methylumbelliferyl-alpha-d-galactopyranoside into a highly fluorescent product, 4-methylumbelliferone (Sigma-Aldrich). After adding glycine-NaOH, pH 10.7, to terminate the reaction, fluorescence was measured using SpectraMax iD3 (excitation, 365 nm; emission, 450 nm). The fluorescence count was converted into 4-methylumbelliferone concentration (nM) by comparison to the standard curve, which was prepared by serial dilution of 100 mM 4-methylumbelliferone solution. Then, the 4-methylumbelliferone concentration was converted into cellular alpha-GAL activity.
Bioinformatic analysis of RNA-seq data

RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) data were mapped to the human genome sequence (GRCh38) using STAR (version 2.7.1a). Ensembl gene annotation version 98 was used for the mapping process. For splicing analysis, the rMATS program version 4.1.0 was used. Bam files were preprocessed following a previously described method. After the rMATS calculation, AS events that passed the following criteria were processed as significant AS events: FDR < 0.1, related reads >=8 in either of the splicing forms, and ldPSIl >= 0.20.
Immunocytostaining

Cells were fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde (Nacalai Tesque, 09154-85) in Dulbecco's PBS (D-PBS) for 5 min, permeabilized with 0.1% saponin (Sigma-Aldrich) in D-PBS for 15 min, and then blocked with 3% bovine serum albumin (BSA; Nacalai Tesque, 19361-84) in D-PBS. Cells were incubated with the primary antibodies diluted in 3% BSA in D-PBS for 30 min, washed twice with D-PBS for 5 min each, and then incubated with the secondary antibodies for 30 min. The cells were washed twice with D-PBS again and observed under a fluorescence microscope (Keyence) with counterstaining with Hoechst 33342 (Themo Fisher Scientific). The antibodies used were as follows: anti-cardiac troponin T rabbit polyclonal antibody (Abcam), anti-LAMP1 rabbit polyclonal antibody (Abcam), anti-Gb3 mouse monoclonal antibody (Tokyo Chemical Industry, Tokyo, Japan), Alexa Fluor 488-conjugated anti-rabbit IgG antibody (Thermo Fisher Scientific), and Alexa Fluor 555-conjugated anti-mouse IgG antibody (Thermo Fisher Scientific). The cells were then observed with a fluorescence microscope (Keyence) and analyzed for fluorescence intensities with a BZ-X analyzer and hybrid cell count software (Keyence). For the Gb3 deposition assay, the accumulated intensity of Alexa Fluor 555-labeled Gb3 inside the Alexa Fluor 488-labeled cardiac troponin T-positive area was divided by the Alexa Fluor 488-labeled cardiac troponin T-positive area. Values were normalized to the mean of wt/DMSO.
Pharmacokinetics

The protocol for the pharmacokinetic analysis of RECTAS-2.0 was as follows. Nine-week-old C57BL/6 mice (n = 2) were p.o. administered 0.5% methylcellulose-suspended compounds at 10 mg/kg-BW. Blood samples were obtained at 0.25, 0.5, 1, 2, 4, 7, and 24 hours after administration. Kp for plasma versus heart drug delivery was determined on the basis of compound concentrations in plasma and heart tissue 0.5 hours after the p.o. administration of 30 mg/kg-BW. The animal protocol was conducted at Daiichi Sankyo Co. Ltd. (Tokyo, Japan) under approval from the institutional ethical committee.
Preclinical safety evaluation

For toxicokinetic study, 6-week-old male rats [Crl: CD(SD)] were administered vehicle (0.5% MC) or RECTAS-2.0 (100, 300, or 1000 mg/kg-BW) p.o. (n = 6 for each group). General conditions were analyzed 24 hours later, followed by euthanasia for necropsy. Plasma concentration of RECTAS-2.0 was conducted in Daiichi Sankyo Co. Ltd. Toxicokinetic study of RECTAS-2.0 was outsourced to Nihon Bioresearch Inc. (Gifu, Japan), under approval from the institutional ethical committee, following the guidelines of the Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare of Japan. For the Langendorff heart test, 10-week-old female rabbits (Kbl: NZW) were used for the preparation of Langendorff hearts for ex vivo functional evaluation. Rabbits were euthanized with anesthesia using thiopental sodium, heart tissues were excised, and Langendorff hearts were constructed and treated with vehicle [0.1% (v/v) DMSO] or RECTAS-2.0 (3, 10, and 30 muM) for 15 min. During incubation with vehicle or RECTAS-2.0, acute effects on heart functions were evaluated using a DAM50 extracellular amplifier (World Precision Instruments Inc., Sarasota, FL, USA) and Pressure Monitor 4 (Living Systems Instrumentation, St. Albans City, VT, USA). The electrocardiogram was recorded and analyzed with the Iox2 and ecgAUTO3 system (Emka Technologies, Osaka, Japan). Langendorff heart test was conducted by the Safety Research Institute for Chemical Compounds Co. Ltd. (Hokkaido, Japan), under approval from the institutional ethical committee and following the guidelines of the Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare, and the Ministry of the Environment, Japan. To investigate the effect of RECTAS-2.0 on human ether-a-go-go related gene (hERG) potassium current, high-throughput screening assay was conducted using SyncroPatch 384PE (Nanion Technologies GmbH) and recombinant HEK293 cell line introduced with hERG (SB Drug Discovery Limited). For the Ames test, Salmonella typhimurium or Escherichia coli strains were incubated with control compound 2AA or RECTAS-2.0 for 48 hours at 37 C in the presence of S9 mix (n = 2 for each condition). Colonies with reverse mutation were detected using a CC-1 colony counter (ASONE, Osaka, Japan) for RECTAS-2.0 and a CA-11D colony analyzer (System Science Co. Ltd., Tokyo, Japan) for 2AA. The Ames test was outsourced to Nihon Bioresearch Inc.
Transgenic mice

The GLA construct for transgenic mice was prepared as follows. A coding sequence (NCBI: NM_000169.3) with insertion of the c.639+919G>A-mutated intron 4 was designed to be transcribed through the CMV enhancer/IE promoter and an SV40 polyadenylation signal, using pAcGFP-N1 mammalian expression vector (Takara Bio) as a parental construct. The vector construct was then digested with ApaLI and DraIII-HF (New England Biolabs, Ipswich, MA, USA), and the resulting linearized GLA fragment was applied for pronuclear injection to fertilized eggs of a C57BL/6J mouse. The primer set oAM81 and oAM58, yielding a 1.6-kb product, was used for screening a founder and genotyping PCR for tail snips. For GLA splicing assessment in heart tissue, 8-week-old male mice were used. Male mice were used because, in humans, FD predominantly affects males. RECTAS or RECTAS-2.0 was suspended in 0.5% methylcellulose solution, orally administered (0 and 100 mg/kg-BW for RECTAS, and 0, 30, and 100 mg/kg-BW for RECTAS-2.0), and then administered again at the same dose 3 hours later. Three hours after the second administration, the mice were euthanized and their heart tissues were excised. Excised heart tissues were immediately minced, rinsed in PBS, immersed in TRIzol reagent (Thermo Fisher Scientific), and snap-frozen in liquid nitrogen, until subsequent RNA extraction. For ex vivo assessment of compound response, GLA c.639+919G>A transgenic mice were anesthetized with isoflurane, and peripheral blood was collected from the maxillary vein with an animal lancet. A total of 150 mul of collected blood was incubated with heparin at a final concentration of 10 mug/ml, followed by addition of the same volume of RPMI1640, supplemented with 10% FBS and 1% PS. Blood cells were then incubated at 37 C with 5% CO2 and incubated with CHX at a final concentration of 100 mug/ml for 6 hours. Next, RNA extraction was conducted using a NucleoSpin RNA blood column (Takara Bio) and Direct-zol RNA Miniprep (Zymo Research). The mice were euthanized using carbon dioxide in accordance with the American Veterinary Medical Association guidelines on euthanasia. The animal study protocol was approved by the institutional ethical committee of Kyoto University Graduate School of Medicine, and conducted in accordance with Animal Research: Reporting of In Vivo Experiments guidelines.

passages.text: Quantitative Proteomics and Phosphoproteomics Analysis of Patient-Derived Ovarian Cancer Stem Cells

High-grade serous ovarian carcinoma (HGSOC) is the deadliest gynecologic cancer. Key to the progression and ultimate lethality of this subtype is the intra-tumoral heterogeneity, which is defined as the coexistence of different cell types and populations within a single tumor. Among those, ovarian cancer stem cells (OCSCs) are a distinct subpopulation of tumor cells endowed with stem-like properties, which can survive current standard therapies, resulting in tumor recurrence. Here, we generated ex vivo primary OCSC-enriched three-dimensional (3D) spheres from 10 distinct treatment naive patient-derived adherent (2D) cultures. We used state-of-the-art quantitative mass spectrometry to characterize the molecular events associated with OCSCs by analyzing their proteome and phosphoproteome. Our data revealed a stemness-related protein signature, shared within a heterogeneous patient cohort, which correlates with chemo-refractoriness in a clinical proteomics dataset. Moreover, we identified targetable deregulated kinases and aberrant PDGF receptor activation in OCSCs. Pharmacological inhibition of PDGFR in adherent OC cells reduced the stemness potential, measured by sphere formation assay. Overall, we provide a valuable resource to identify new OCSC markers and putative targets for OCSC-directed therapies.
Graphical Abstract
Highlights
Mass spectrometry reveals a conserved stemness signature in ovarian cancer.
Stemness proteins are involved in extracellular matrix remodeling and metabolism.
The stemness signature correlates with chemo-refractoriness in clinical datasets.
Aberrant PDGF receptor activation is a key feature of ovarian cancer stemness.
PDGFR inhibition reduces stemness potential in patient-derived cancer cells.
In Brief

A quantitative mass spectrometry-based proteomics and phosphoproteomics analysis revealed a conserved protein signature of patient-derived ovarian cancer stem cells (OCSCs). This stemness-related signature correlated with chemo-refractoriness in a clinical proteomics dataset. Moreover, we found an aberrant activation of the PDGF receptor in OCSCs and showed that pharmacological inhibition of PDGFR reduced stemness potential. Our data unveiled new stemness-associated markers and pathways, as well as putative vulnerabilities for OCSCtargeted treatments.

Ovarian cancer (OC) comprises a heterogeneous group of malignancies caused by abnormal cell growth either in the ovaries, fallopian tubes or endometrium. Epithelial ovarian cancer (EOC) represents almost 90% of all cases, which are further classified into several subtypes. High-grade serous ovarian carcinoma (HGSOC) is the most common and lethal subtype of EOC; it arises from either the fallopian tube or the ovarian surface epithelium and accounts for the majority of ovarian cancer-related deaths, with a 5-years survival rate below 30%. The high mortality rate is mainly due to the lack of efficient tools for early diagnosis and to the lack of effective treatment options for advanced-stage disease. Therefore, understanding the molecular mechanisms of OC development and progression represents a critical step to improving patient survival.

Tumors are composed of heterogeneous cell populations. Among these, cancer stem cells (CSCs) represent a rare population of cells, derived from either the malignant transformation of a normal stem cell or the dedifferentiation of a mature cancer cell, that are responsible for giving rise to the whole tumor. The main features of CSCs are self-renewal, clonogenic potential, resistance to anoikis, quiescent state, acquisition of epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) traits, ability to undergo differentiation through asymmetric cell division and resistance to chemotherapy. In addition, CSCs can generate a tumor upon transplantation into a recipient organism. Based on this function, CSCs are also commonly called tumor-initiating cells (TICs). The role of CSCs in tumor initiation and recurrence, as well as chemoresistance, makes them the ideal drug target for tumor eradication.

Proteomics is the large-scale analysis of proteins in a biological sample and has been previously employed to study OC biology. The Clinical Proteomic Tumor Analysis Consortium (CPTAC) thoroughly investigated the impact of genomic alterations on cancer biology at a functional level by comprehensively analyzing a large number of HGSOC specimens by mass spectrometry (MS)-based proteomics, glycoproteomics and phosphoproteomics. However, these studies employed bulk tumor samples, losing cell identity information. Laser-capture microdissection combined with MS-based proteomics has been successfully used to separately analyze tumor cells and stroma in HGSOC. Still, information about proteome changes between differentiated tumor cells and their stem cell counterparts is not yet available.

Biological properties of CSCs are intrinsically difficult to assess within the original tumor, due to the lack of general and robust markers. Sphere formation under non-adherent conditions is a cell-based assay, which allows enrichment for CSCs as it exploits their ability to resist anoikis and generate clonal spheroidal colonies. To characterize the molecular traits of CSCs from HGSOC (ovarian CSCs, OCSCs), in this study we generated patient-derived primary cultures from HGSOC peritoneal ascites, which are known to be enriched in tumor cells with stem-like properties, as tumor cells in this location survive and proliferate as spheres in the absence of adhesion. We performed quantitative MS-based proteomics and phosphoproteomics on cells either grown as adherent two-dimensional (2D) cultures or as non-adherent stem-cell enriched three-dimensional (3D) spheres. We showed that OCSCs exhibit homogeneous proteome and phosphoproteome signatures, which can potentially be exploited to define specific molecular markers and develop OCSC-targeted therapies.
Experimental Procedures
Primary Cells

All ascites samples were obtained upon informed consent from women undergoing surgery at the Gynecology Division of the European Institute of Oncology and collected via standardized operative procedures approved by the Institutional Ethical Board (European Institute of Oncology). Tumor histology was confirmed by a board-certified pathologist (G. Bertalot), while the identity of cancer cells was confirmed by immunostaining for cytokeratins 5, 7 and 8, or pan-cytokeratins. The purity of primary cell culture was consistently over 95%. Tissue isolation and culture conditions of primary cells were performed as described previously. This study was conducted in compliance with the principles of the Declaration of Helsinki.
Sphere Formation Assay

Sphere formation assays were performed as described previously. Briefly, single-cell suspensions were obtained from trypsinization of primary cultures and seeded at low density (5000 cells/ml) under non-adherent conditions in poly-(2-hydroxyethyl methacrylate)-coated dishes (Sigma-Aldrich, cat# P3932) and allowed to form clonal spheres. CSC-enriched sphere were maintained in MEBM (Lonza, cat# CC-3151), supplemented with 2% B27 (Thermo Fisher Scientific, cat# 17504044;), 2 mM L-glutamine, 100 U/ml penicillin, 100 mug/ml streptomycin, 5 mug/ml insulin (Thermo Fisher Scientific, cat# RP10935), 0.5 mug/ml hydrocortisone (Sigma-Aldrich, cat# H0888), 1 U/ml heparin (Voden, cat # 07980), 20 ng/ml epidermal growth factor (EGF, Merck, cat# E4127) and 20 ng/ml fibroblast growth factor-2 (FGF2; Peprotech, cat# AF-100-18B).

Sphere formation was assessed 5 to 10 days after seeding. Spheres were then dissociated with StemPro Accutase (Thermo Fisher Scientific, cat# A1110501), according to the manufacturer's protocol, and re-plated under the same conditions for 72 h to obtain second-generation spheres, which were then used for MS analysis.

PDGFR inhibitors were purchased from Merck Life Science (Axitinib: cat. No. PZ0193; Imatinib Mesylate: cat. No. SML1027). The inhibitor was added when seeding the cells for the second-generation spheres and maintained for the entire duration of the sphere formation assay (72 h).
Immunoblotting
Spheres and 2D cells were lysed in hot lysis buffer (2.5% SDS, 125 mM Tris-HCl [pH 6.8]), after 15 min incubation at 95  C.

Protein concentration was determined using a Pierce BCA Protein Assay kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Inc, cat# 23227) according to the manufacturer's instructions. Equal amounts of protein extracts (20 mug) were resolved in acrylamide gel and transferred onto nitrocellulose membranes. The membranes were incubated overnight at 4  C with the following primary antibodies: GPNMB (LSBio, cat# LS-B11132), CHI3L1 (R&D Systems, cat# AF2599), phospho-PDGFR beta tyrosine-1009 (Cell Signaling Technology, cat# 3124), PDGFR beta (Cell Signaling Technology cat# #4564), GAPDH (Sigma-Aldrich, cat# ABS16), and vinculin (Sigma-Aldrich, cat# V9131). Membranes were incubated with HRP-conjugated secondary antibody (Bio-Rad Laboratories) for 1 h at room temperature. The signal was detected by the Clarity Western ECL Substrate (Bio-Rad, cat# 1705062) following the manufacturer's protocol and the images were acquired using ChemiDoc (Bio-Rad).

Immunofluorescence

Cultured adherent cells or cytospins with spheres were fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde for 5 min at room temperature and then permeabilized in ice-cold PBS, 0.5% Triton X-100 for 3 min at 4   C. After blocking for 1 h at room temperature with blocking buffer (PBS, 0.2% BSA, 1% donkey serum, 0.05% Tween-20 and 0.02% NaN3), cells were incubated for 2 h with the following primary antibodies, diluted in blocking buffer: anti-CD73 (clone AA60E3.3), generated by E. Dejana (Milan) and produced by the Biochemistry Unit at Cogentech, Milan; anti-CD24 (BD Biosciences, catalog no. 555427); anti-CD106 (BD Biosciences, catalog no. 555647); anti-CD44 (clone Hermes-3, from U. Gunthert, Basel).

Cells were then washed with PBS and incubated with the Alexa Fluor-conjugated secondary antibodies (Jackson Laboratories) for 1 h at room temperature. Nuclei were counterstained with DAPI (Sigma-Aldrich, cat# 32670). Images were acquired using the Leica SP8 Confocal microscope.
Cell Lysis, Protein Extraction and Digestion for Mass Spectrometry

Cells were lysed with boiling guanidine-hydrochloride lysis buffer (6M Gnd-HCl, 100 mM Tris-HCl pH 8.5, 5 TCEP, 10 mM CAA). Lysates were heated at 95  C for 10 min, while shaking. Samples were diluted with 25 mM Tris-HCl pH 8.5 to reach a Gnd-HCl concentration of 1M and sonicated (Vibra-Cell VCX130, Sonics) for 2 min, with pulses of 1 s on and 1 s off. Protein concentration was determined using the Bradford assay (Bio-Rad). Proteins were pre-digested with endoproteinase Lys-C (Wako) for 2 h at room temperature in an enzyme/protein ratio of 1:100 before overnight digestion with trypsin (Sigma-Aldrich) at 37  C in an enzyme/protein ratio of 1:50. After overnight digestion, enzymatic activity was quenched by acidifying the lysates using trifluoroacetic acid (TFA) at a final concentration of 1% and ensuring the pH of the samples being around 2. Precipitates were removed by centrifugation at 3000g for 5 min.
750 ng of digested peptides for single-shot proteome analysis were loaded on C18 Evotips (Evosep) for MS analysis. Two technical replicates per sample were prepared.

Digested peptides for TMT labeling were purified and concentrated on reversed-phase C18 Sep-Pak cartridges (Waters). After elution with 40% acetonitrile (ACN) followed by 60% ACN, a SpeedVac concentrator (ThermoFisher Scientific), operating at 60  C, was utilized to concentrate the samples. Peptide concentration was estimated by measuring absorbance at 280 nm (A280) on a NanoDrop spectrophotometer (ThermoFisher Scientific).
TMT labeling

For TMT-labeling (11-plex kit, Thermo Fisher Scientific) of samples, 28 mug of peptides per sample were used. A pooled sample for normalization between TMTs was prepared by combining 2.8 mug of peptide from each individual sample. Labeling was performed according to the manufacturer's instructions. All samples were adjusted to a concentration of 50% ACN and alkalized to a pH of 8 using HEPES, for a final concentration of 30 mM. The labeling reaction between the peptides and the TMT reagents was conducted over 1 h using 3 mul TMT reagent per sample. The reaction was then quenched for 15 min using 1% hydroxylamine (1:1 hydroxylamine:TMT), after which the samples were pulled, acidified and ACN was then evaporated in the SpeedVac concentrator. TMT labeled peptides were purified on reversed-phase C18 Sep-Pak cartridges (Waters). After elution with 40% acetonitrile (ACN) followed by 60% and 80% ACN, the SpeedVac concentrator was used to concentrate the samples to reach a volume below 25 ul.

Patients 1 to 5 comprised the first TMT-plex, and patients 6 to 10 comprised the second TMT-plex. The 11th channel 131C is the reference channel and is made by a pool of all 20 samples (see supplemental Table S7 for the detailed TMT labeling scheme).
Enrichment of Phosphorylated Peptides

Ti-IMAC phosphopeptide enrichment was carried out on a KingFisher Flex robot (Thermo Fisher Scientific) in 96-well format, as previously described. 308 mug of peptide were used for enrichments, with 30 mul of magnetic Ti-IMAC HP beads (ReSyn Biosciences). The 96-well comb is stored in plate #1, Ti-IMAC HP beads in 100% ACN in plate #2 and loading buffer (1 M glycolic acid, 80% ACN, 5% TFA) in plate #3. The sample is mixed with loading buffer and added in plate #4. Plates 5 to 7 are filled with 500 mul of washing solutions (loading buffer, 80% ACN, 5% TFA, and 10% ACN, 0.2% TFA, respectively). Plate #8 contains 200 mul of 1% NH4OH for elution. The beads are washed in loading buffer for 5 min at medium mixing speed, followed by binding of the phosphopeptides for 20 min and medium speed. The sequential washes are performed in 2 min and fast speed. Phosphopeptides are eluted in 10 min at medium mixing speed.
High-pH Reversed-phase Stage-Tip Fractionation of Phosphopeptides

Labeled phosphopeptides were manually fractionated using high-pH reversed-phase chromatography in stage-tips, as previously described. In-house stage tips were prepared using low-bind 200 mul tips with three discs of 3M Empore C18 (Waters). Stage tips were conditioned with 50 mul methanol, 50 mul of 20 mM ammonia in ACN, 2 x 100 mul 20 mM ammonia in water. Phosphopeptides were loaded 3 times on the tip. 50 mul of 20 mM ammonia in water was loaded on the tip and combined with the flow through (FT). The peptides were eluted successively with 4, 8, 12, 20, 80% ACN with 20 mM ammonia. The two last fractions were pooled together. ACN was evaporated and the samples acidified with formic acid (pH < 3) before being loaded on C18 Evotips (Evosep) for MS analysis.
Mass Spectrometry Analysis

Samples were analyzed on the Evosep One LC system coupled to an Orbitrap Exploris 480. Samples were separated on an in-house packed 15 cm analytical column (150 mum inner diameter), packed with 1.9 mum C18 beads, and the column temperature was maintained at 60  C using an integrated column oven (PRSO-V1, Sonation GmbH). Pre-programmed gradients were used: 30 samples per day for proteome (SPD), and 60 SPD for phosphoproteome.

The mass spectrometer was operated in positive ion mode, with spray voltage at 2 kV, heated capillary temperature at 275  C, and funnel RF frequency at 40. The Peptide match was set to off, and isotope exclusion was on. We used data-independent acquisition (DIA) for label-free total proteome and data-dependent acquisition mode (DDA) for TMT-labeled samples, respectively.

For DIA, full MS resolution was set to 120,000 at m/z 200 and normalized AGC target was set at 300%, with an injection time of 45 ms, and the precursor scan range was set to 361 to 1033 m/z. The MS/MS acquisition was set to 15,000 resolution, and injection time to 22 ms; normalized collision energy was set at 27%; normalized AGC target value was set at 1000%; 49 windows of 13.7 m/z were used with an overlap of 1 Da.

For DDA, full MS resolution was set to 60,000 at m/z 200 and normalized AGC target was set at 300%, with an injection time of 25 ms, and the precursor scan range was set to 350 to 1400 m/z. The MS/MS acquisition was set to 15,000 resolution, and injection time to 22 ms; normalized collision energy was set at 35%; normalized AGC target value was set at 200%; isolation window was set at 0.8 m/z; dynamic exclusion was set at 30 s; intensity threshold was set at 2E5; a Top12 method was used; the turbo-TMT (centroid mode) was enabled.
Mass Spectrometry Raw Data Processing

DIA data were analyzed on Spectronaut version 18 in directDIA mode with the standard settings. The Human Uniprot fasta file (downloaded in March 2023; 20,422 entries) was supplemented with a contaminant fasta file containing 370 entries, downloaded from:

https://github.com/HaoGroup-ProtContLib. Carbamidomethyl was set as a fixed modification, and N-terminal acetylation and oxidation of methionine as variable modifications. Up to five variable modifications were allowed. Trypsin was set as cleavage enzyme with a maximum of two missed cleavages. The mass tolerance was set to dynamic in both MS1 and MS2 level with a correction factor of 1. A Q value of 1% against mutated decoys was applied to filter identifications with a false-discovery rate level of 0.01 at both the peptide and protein level. Quantification was performed using the automatic setting, which was Quant 2.0 in this Spectronaut version. Cross-run normalization and imputation were not enabled, with the exception of the PDGFRB precursor analysis (supplemental Fig. S14C).

TMT phosphoproteome raw MS data were analyzed using the MaxQuant software, version 2.6.6.0, with the integrated Andromeda search engine. Files were searched against a target/decoy version of the human UniProt database (downloaded in May 2024; 20,434 entries). The UniProt database version was supplemented with the MaxQuant contaminant list. Carbamidomethyl was set as a fixed modification; oxidation of methionine, N-terminal acetylation, deamidation of asparagine and glutamine, and phosphorylation of serine, threonine, and tyrosine were included as variable modifications. A maximum of four variable modifications and two miscleavages were allowed per peptide. The precursor mass tolerance was set to 20 ppm, and the initial fragment mass tolerance was set to 0.6 Da. A false discovery rate of 1% was applied for peptide, protein and site identifications. TMT correction factors were not used. Channel 11 was set as the reference channel. Normalization was set to "weighted ratio to reference channel". The isobaric weight exponent was set to 0.75 (standard setting). Match between runs was enabled with the standard settings, with the only exception of the matching time window that was set to 0.7 min.

To calculate TMT labeling efficiency, TMT126C was set as a variable modification, both at lysine residues and the N-terminal, together with phosphorylation of serine, threonine, and tyrosine. Carbamidomethyl was set as a fixed modification. A maximum of five variable modifications and one miscleavage were allowed per peptide.
Bioinformatic Analysis

Data analysis was done using the R software package v4.4.1 (with RStudio v2024.09.0) and the Perseus Software v1.6.15. The majority of plots were performed using the "ggplot2" R package. Heatmaps were performed using the "pheatmap" R package and the clustering was performed using Euclidean distance, unless stated otherwise.
Proteome Data

Protein groups' MS intensities were log2-transformed to stabilize the variance. Data were filtered by removing potential contaminants and entries without gene names. Data normalization was performed by median realignment: the median of all proteins of a run was subtracted from each protein intensity of the corresponding run; then, the mean of the 40 medians was summed to each value. Afterward, technical replicates (2 MS injections per sample) were averaged.
Principal component analysis was performed after removing all missing values; data were centered but not scaled. The PCA plot were performed through the "ggbiplot" R package.

We considered a protein as unique to OCSCs if it had no values in all patients (=10) in the bulk condition, but had at least four valid values in OCSCs. Conversely, we considered a protein as unique to the bulk condition if it had no values in all patients (=10) in the OCSCs, but had at least four valid values in the bulk condition.

Before differential expression analysis, data were filtered by requiring at least three valid values per group (bulk and OCSCs). Differential expression analysis was performed by using the "Limma" R package, accounting for paired measurements (blocking on the patient). p values were corrected by using the Benjamini-Hochberg (BH) procedure. The fold-change was calculated as mean(protein X)OCSC - mean(protein X)bulk in log2 space. A fold-change cutoff was calculated separately for up- and down-regulated proteins as +-2x standard deviation of fold-changes. The calculated fold-change cutoff was equal to 0.89 for up- and -0.7 for down-regulated proteins. Proteins were considered significantly regulated if their adjusted p value was <= 0.01 and their fold-change exceeded the calculated fold-change cutoff.

Gene ontology (GO) and pathway enrichment analyses were performed against the whole dataset as background. The input protein list included all up-regulated/down-regulated proteins as defined above plus all proteins unique to OCSCs/bulk, respectively. GO enrichment was performed with the "topGO" R package with the ontologies biological processes (BP) and cellular components (CC). Fisher's exact test with the "weight01" algorithm was used. Node size was set to five for BP and to 10 for CC. p values were corrected by using the BH procedure. KEGG and Reactome pathway enrichment analyses were performed with the R packages "clusterProfiler" and "ReactomePA". Gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) was performed through clusterProfiler by using the molecular signature database (MSigDB). Proteins were ranked by fold-change OCSCs vs bulk.

Functional protein networks displayed were generated through STRING and the "Omics Visualizer" app for Cytoscape. Proteins used for this analysis belong to the GO terms highlighted in blue in supplemental Figs. S7 and S8 and are listed in supplemental Table S8.

Hierarchical clustering analysis of fold-changes OCSCs vs bulk was performed using Euclidean distance to define clusters of patients. To find proteins with significantly different fold-change between the two clusters, we applied the Mann-Whitney U Test. Proteins with a p value < 0.02 were considered for further analysis.
Processing of Proteomics Data From Other Publications for Single-Sample Gene Set Enrichment Analysis (ssGSEA)
Proteome data from Yang et al. and Chowdhury et al. were downloaded from the respective publications.

In the dataset from Yang et al., murine gene IDs were converted to human IDs using the R package "homologene". Proteins without a human homolog were discarded. Intensities of proteins with the same gene ID were averaged. Pooled samples were removed. Proteins with more than 30% of missing values across the dataset were removed. Log2 intensities were normalized by median realignment through the R package "DAPAR". Missing values were considered missing not at random (MNAR) and imputed using QRILC from the R package "imputeLCMD".
In the dataset from Chowdhury et al., patient samples analyzed multiple times in different TMT plexes were averaged.
Gene sets for ssGSEA were created using significantly regulated proteins and proteins completely missing in one condition (attached in txt format as supplemental Table S9).
ssGSEA was performed on Gene Pattern with default settings.
Phosphoproteome Data
Enrichment and labeling efficiency per TMT-plex were calculated by using the MaxQuant table "modificationSpecificPeptides".

The "Phospho (STY)Sites" table from MaxQuant was used for bioinformatic analysis, after applying the "expand the site table" function implemented in Perseus. MS intensities were Log2-transformed and filtered by removing reverse hits, potential contaminants, rows without a gene name and rows without any quantification value. Phosphorylation sites with a localization score <0.75 were excluded. MS reporter intensities were normalized by quantile-based normalization, performed through the "Limma" R package.
Differential expression analysis was performed as discussed above for the proteome data. Fold-change cutoffs were equal to 0.84 for up- and -0.71 for down-regulated proteins.

Kinase enrichment analysis was performed by using the RoKAI web tool (https://rokai.io), version 2.3.0. As input, the logFC calculated by Limma was used. Values from the same site and different multiplicities were averaged. The fold-change was set on "raw" and phosphatases were not included. Kinases were considered regulated if the p value was <=0.05 and the substrates were >=3.

Normalization on the proteome level was performed by subtracting the protein intensity from the corresponding phosphorylation sites (in log2 space). Both datasets were first normalized as described above.
Kaplan-Meier Survival Curves
Kaplan-Meier survival curves were performed through the web-based tool KM plotter (https://kmplot.com), using mRNA gene chip data for ovarian cancer.
Experimental Design and Statistical Rationale

In this study, different individuals are considered as biological replicates. The number of biological replicates (=10) was set based on the availability of appropriate samples in the biobank. For the proteome analysis, technical replicates were acquired (the same sample was injected twice in the MS). These were averaged before statistical analysis. Since the aim of this study was to identify differences between spheres and bulk, a paired design was employed (blocking on the individual).
