passages.text: Management of radioresistance in cancer

The stage in which cancer/tumor cells or tissues adapt to the radiation conditions and show resistance to radiation therapy-promoted changes is called radioresistance. Radioresistance occurs due to increased DNA lesion repair, which protects the cells from genomic instability. Alterations in oncogene/tumor suppressor genes, such as dysregulation of vitronectin, an oncogene, induce the invasion and migration of cancer cells. Alterations in miR-29c and miR-22 expression are also involved in radio resistance. The tumor microenvironment (TME), such as cytokine levels and hypoxic conditions, can also induce radioresistance. Decreased autophagy in tumor cells, generation of cancer stem cells (CSCs), and alterations in tumor metabolism are associated with radioresistance. Huang et al. reported that suppression/blocking of mitochondrial ATP-sensitive potassium channels (mtKATP) can alleviate the radioresistance of glioma by inhibiting ROS-induced activation of ERK. This indicates that mtKATP channel inactivators and MAPK/ERK kinase (MEK) suppressors could be efficient drug targets for alleviating radioresistance. Pan et al. reported that the radioresistant subtypes, A549 R and H460 R, were irradiated with hypofractionated radiation and treated with erastin, and found that erastin treatment increased the radiosensitivity of radioresistant cells and inhibited GPX4 expression. Erastin, in combination with ionizing radiation, resulted in increased cell death compared to treatment with erastin or ionizing radiation alone. This indicates that the suppression of radioresistance in NSCLC cells is elicited by promoting GPx4- mediated ferroptosis. Park et al. reported that low-dose radiation (LDR) pretreatment of NSCLC cells results in overexpression of miR-30a and miR-30b that can inhibit plasminogen activator inhibitor-1 (PAI-1). Akt and ERK phosphorylation were also found to be decreased by PAI-1 inhibition. They also used 7C1 lipid-based nanoparticles to encapsulate miR-30a and miR-30b into an orthotopic mouse xenograft model, and found decreased tumor growth and aggressiveness by pre-LDR followed by radiation therapy. Hypoxic subvolumes, found in cancer stem cell subpopulation, and radioresistance that can be present inherently or acquired.They indicate aggressiveness of tumour and their potential to undergo metastasis making it a great challenge in cancer therapy. Spatially fractionated radiation therapy (SFRT) is also recently used to tackle major challenges offering high therapeutic index for radioresistant tumor treatment. Noncoding RNAs have also shown promising results in the management of prostate cancer.
Nuclear disaster of Hiroshima, Nagasaki and Chernobyl and their impact

Researchers have recently outlined the long-term radiological impacts, psychosocial effects, and infrastructure response following Chernobyl and Fukushima accidents. There has also been a review of the studies that investigated radiation-related effects in offspring of radiation-exposed individuals published between 2018 and 2022. A nuclear weapon was used for the first time in war on 6 August 1945, in Hiroshima and on 9 August 1945, in Nagasaki. New weapons of mass destruction were introduced to the world as a result of the devastation caused in the two cities. In spite of the fact that reported numbers vary, it is estimated that by the end of 1945, 90,000 to 120,000 civilians out of a civilian population of about 330,000 in Hiroshima, as well as 60,000 to 80,000 people out of 280,000 in Nagasaki, would be dead as a result of being exposed to the intense heat, physical force, and ionizing radiation emitted by the bombs. The scientists affiliated to Atomic Bomb Casualty Commission and their successor institute, the Radiation Effects Research Foundation, assessed the long-term health effects for the past 63 years in the surviving population of the atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki as well as in their offsprings. Long-term, large-scale epidemiological studies have shown that ionizing radiation causes late-onset effects on the human body. Because of the size of the cohort, exposure of both sexes and all ages, and the wide range of individually assessed doses, the cohort study of Japanese survivors of the atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki (the Life Span Study) is considered the most reliable source of information about these health effects. Radiation-induced cancer is clearly associated with survivors having a higher cancer risk than older survivors. Children exposed to radiation are at higher risk than those exposed as adults. The risk of cardiovascular disease and some other non-cancer diseases may be increased by radiation at high doses, and possibly at low doses as well. Although, survivors of the atomic bomb have not been reported to have inherited any hereditary effects.

In the past few decades, Chernobyl, which sits 130 kilometers north of the Ukrainian capital Kiev and ten kilometers south of the Belarusian border, has been the scene of some of the most serious nuclear accidents in history. The power plant was destroyed by two violent explosions on 26 April 1986, causing a series of fires and releasing radioactive materials into the atmosphere. Finely fragmented nuclear fuel particles, gases, and aerosols were released. When it comes to radionuclides, iodine-131 and cesium-137 are of the utmost importance. Wind directions changed frequently during the massive releases, so all areas around the reactor received fallout at some point during the 10 days. Furthermore, rainfall occurred irregularly, resulting in different degrees of deposition. All countries in the Northern Hemisphere were contaminated by radioactive materials to some extent due to the releases of radioactive material. Nevertheless, Belarus, Russia, and Ukraine are the countries most affected by contamination.

Ten years after Chernobyl, the health status of the residents was reviewed. There were apparently fewer than 100 deaths within the first few months as a result of acute radiation damage due to high doses of ionizing radiation. There has been no evidence of an increase in congenital abnormalities, except perhaps for Down's syndrome. Belarus and Ukraine, as well as the Bryansk region of Russia, have already seen dramatic increases in childhood thyroid cancers. A few areas with heavy contamination have seen an increase of over 100-fold.

The fallout from Chernobyl accident exposed millions of people to radioactive isotopes twenty years after the accident. As yet, there has not been a general increase in malignancies over the past 20 years, although thyroid carcinoma incidence has increased considerably and breast cancer has possibly been affected by radiation. It was first noticed in children that the iodine 131 release was causing an increase in thyroid carcinoma, associated with a strong relationship between young age when exposed and risk of papillary thyroid carcinoma (PTC). Children exposed to I-131 as children in Ukraine and Belarus have developed PTC, even 30 years after the Chernobyl disaster. Chromosome rearrangements and gene fusions in post-Chernobyl PTCs have provided new information important to molecular mechanisms. The incidence of thyroid cancer and hematological malignancies in adults has been shown to increase with the exposure level of clean-up workers/liquidators. Cardiovascular and cerebrovascular diseases are also on the rise. These incidents indicate that ionizing radiation caused disaster can cause damage to the genetic level which can be carry forwarded for generations after generations.

For many decades, it has been recognized that radiation exposure during the development of an embryo or fetus can result in two major types of severe health effects: it can disrupt normal intrauterine development, or it may lead to the onset of leukemia and cancer during childhood. Recent epidemiological and experimental data have been presented that could enhance our understanding of the underlying mechanisms and help establish radiation protection standards. However, ecological studies of populations exposed to higher radiation levels due to contamination from reactor accidents (such as Chernobyl and Fukushima) have not provided solid evidence to support this goal. In contrast, well-designed experimental studies have demonstrated the multifactorial mechanisms that lead to various health effects following in utero radiation exposure.
Effect on health and biological macromolecules induced by non-ionizing radiation

There are several health scares associated with the electromagnetic radiation generated by radio-based stations, mobile phones, and phone towers, as well as high-voltage power lines, which are associated with health problems such as cancer in humans, and adverse effects on birds, animals, etc.. Oxidative stress have also been reported to be induced by non-ionizing radiations, and sometimes can cause cancer. Thermal and non-thermal effects of non-ionizing radiations of low intensity have also been reported. As the use of mobile phones increases, non-ionizing electromagnetic waves of radio frequencies are generated. Even in the literature, mixed reports are available regarding the long-term use of mobile phones and their association with an elevated risk of cancer. The non-thermal radio frequency impact of mobile phones is classified as group 2 B (potential human carcinogens), and various reports indicate its risk of inducing cancer/tumors. Olkhovskiy et al. studied the radio frequency of a smartphone on platelet aggregation and found that ADP-induced aggregation of platelets in apparently healthy individuals, as well as ischemic stroke patients, increased, whereas it was suppressed in the blood samples of patients with polycythemia vera. Surveys have been conducted by researchers among the college students to know whether they are aware of the ill effects of mobile usage.

Several studies have demonstrated that radiofrequency radiation (RFR) can cause genotoxicity and carcinogenesis, although the results of all of these studies are still controversial. According to one study, exposure limits of (50 Hz, 1800 MHz ELF-EMF), and time were standardized, and the effects of exposure to GSM-Talking mode RF at 50 Hz on mouse spermatocytic cell lines were determined when they were exposed for 24 h to GSM-Talking mode RF at 50 Hz. As shown by alkaline comet assays and immunofluorescence, exposure to low-frequency radio waves resulted in a slight increase in DNA strand breaks, whereas exposure to electromagnetic frequencies had no evident effect on DNA strands.

The direct consequence of solar UV irradiation is that it can generate dimers of cyclobutane pyrimidine (CPD) and pyrimidine 6-4-pyrimidone photoproducts (6-4PP), and UV radiation-induced ROS can damage DNA. Lawrence et al. studied the adverse effects of very-long-wave UVA (>380 nm) and visible radiation (>=400 nm) in vitro and in vivo. They identified various gene expression alterations and protein fold changes both in vitro and in vivo after 24 h and 2 h of exposure, respectively, including dark cyclobutane pyrimidine dimer (CPD) formation. Multiple types of damage are caused by the induction of oxidative stress by chromophores present in the skin, such as alterations in melanin, beta-carotene, and protoporphyrin IX. This shows that there is a need to find an effective sunscreen in the region of UV exposure near 380 nm.

Al Musawi et al. studied the effect of a low-power diode-pumped solid-state (DPSS) laser on serum protein changes. They separated human blood serum and divided it into five groups. Four treatment groups received different doses of DPSS laser (50, 70, 90, and 110 J/cm2) emitting a wavelength of 589 nm, and one group was used as a control. They studied the electrophoretic migration speed of each protein and identified that the electrophoretic migration speed of all the serum proteins decreased, especially at 70 J/cm2. The migration speed of albumin, alpha1, alpha 2, beta, and globulin was significantly decreased. This study showed that laser light with a wavelength of 589 nm could reduce the migration speed of human blood serum proteins. Reports suggest that exposure to blue light-induced retinal damage increases the risk of age-related macular degeneration. R28 cells were irradiated with blue light at 10 mW/cm2, and the blue light exposure decreased cell viability up to 42% and increased apoptosis by 10-fold.

The use of WiFi, also known as wireless local area network (WLAN), which uses a frequency range of 2.400-2.484 and 5.150-5.825 GHz and is a radiofrequency electromagnetic field (RF-EMF), is increasing. The in vitro studies with WiFi (5.8 GHz WiFi of 9.5 V/m for 24 h) on human osteosarcoma (U2OS), mouse embryonic stem cells (IB10), and human fibroblasts (VH10) concluded that WiFi did not show any perturbed cellular processes or pathways in response to WiFi. Another group also tested primary human MRC-5 lung fibroblasts and human trophoblast cells (HTR-8/SVneo) and found no indication of ROS-mediated induction of DNA damage after exposure to WiFi.
Non-ionizing radiation for diagnostics

Dechent et al. studied the characterizing effect of dermoscopy, reflectance confocal microscopy (RCM), and high-frequency ultrasonography (HFUS) in patients with basal cell carcinoma (BCC) before and after treatment (42 Gy in 6 fractions with a brachytherapy device), and the images were taken. A total of 137 imaging assessments were performed in 12 patients before and after treatment with dermoscopy, HFUS, and RCM. Prior to treatment, the presence of BCC-specific characteristics was found to be 91, 81.8, and 17% in images with RCM, dermoscopy, and HFUS, respectively. Images after treatment revealed that the resolution of BCC-specific characteristics was altered by 100, 33.4, and 91.7% from the patient images with RCM, dermoscopy, and HFUS, respectively. Based on this observation, they concluded that RCM is more reliable than dermoscopy and HFUS for the characterization of BCCs' response to radiotherapy.
Non-ionizing radiation for treatment

Various types of radiation have been used to treat various diseases. Chatraie et al. studied the effect of non-thermal plasma on ulcer treatment. In this study, ulcers were created in the dorsal cells of adult rats and treated with plasma for five weeks, at a frequency of 3 days per week. They monitored changes in the histological and mechanical parameters of the treated tissue. Plasma treatment of ulcers was found to improve wound healing, and histological analysis showed that plasma played a significant role in angiogenesis, formation of new hair follicles, re-epithelialization, control of inflammation, and collagen fibrosis. Furthermore, they demonstrated the effect of plasma using mechanical analysis and suggested that plasma treatment can improve tissue tolerance and mechanical strength versus uniaxial tensile load.

Radiation exposure causes energy deposition in the tissues or body parts that are exposed and measured in LET. Humans and animals are exposed to both low and high LET radiation from either natural or manmade sources. Because our body consists of water, exposure to these radiations in aquatic environments causes different types of deleterious effects. Macromolecules, such as DNA, RNA, and proteins, are major targets. In DNA and RNA, radiation exposure can cause strand breaks, base alterations, and mutations, which can lead to organ or cell damage. Although our body has a repair system to repair such damage, its capacity is limited, and it mostly becomes an error-prone repair due to damage overload. Free radicals are generated, which eventually lead to oxidative damage, and chronic low-dose exposure to any oxidant is the etiology of cancer. It is well known that oxidative stress is the root cause of several diseases, such as cardiovascular disease, cancer, ageing, etc., and thus, radiation can contribute to such diseases. At the protein level, radiation can cause damage to amino acids and alter their conformation, causing them to lose their activity. In vivo, ionizing radiation is used to control the growth of uncontrolled proliferating cells, which damages normal cells and is nonspecific. Using nanoparticles, we can target tumor tissues and enhance the effect of radiation in such tissues, causing minimal harm to benign cells. Radioresistance is a major bottleneck in the treatment of cancer. Researchers have proposed that suppression or blocking of mitochondrial ATP-sensitive potassium channels (mtKATP) can improve cellular radioresistance.
Conclusion

In the present review article, we have discussed about the deleterious effect of ionizing and non-ionizing radiations in our body as well as in other animals and cell lines. The different reports suggested that use of ionizing radiation with proper safety measures do not cause any harm, whereas a little breach in safety can lead to disastrous outcomes like Hiroshima and Chernobyl which will be carried out from generations to generations. Treatment of cancer using ionizing radiation is reported to damage the benign cells along with the cancer cells, and it leads to radioresistance. Using nanotechnology, future radiation modality will change giving rise to targeted treatment for cancer. Nano sensitizers and camouflaging cell components act prudently in enhancing the effect of RT as well as disguising their identification by the cancer cells, respectively. Personalized medicine has also come into the treatment filed recently, that can plan a patient specific radiation regime to effectively eradicate the cancer cells and cancer stem cells. Further studies are warranted on approaches for killing cancer stem cells and management of radioresistance in cancer treatment. On the other hand, non-ionizing radiations are also detrimental, causing DNA stand damage and giving birth to harmful free radicals which cause cellular damage. Oxidative stress is the player behind different diseases like cancer, cardiovascular disease, ageing etc., that is elicited by both ionizing and non-ionizing radiation, leading the exposed person to early ageing or death. Antioxidant enzymes like catalase, glutathione peroxidase and superoxide dismutase can scavenge such free radicals which cause the oxidative damage. As a preventive measure to combat the damage caused by the oxidative stress, we have to include antioxidant rich foods and supplements in our diet plan.

passages.text: Multiscale transformers and multi-attention mechanism networks for pathological nuclei segmentation

Pathology nuclei segmentation is crucial of computer-aided diagnosis in pathology. However, due to the high density, complex backgrounds, and blurred cell boundaries, it makes pathology cell segmentation still a challenging problem. In this paper, we propose a network model for pathology image segmentation based on a multi-scale Transformer multi-attention mechanism. To solve the problem that the high density of cell nuclei and the complexity of the background make it difficult to extract features, a dense attention module is embedded in the encoder, which improves the learning of the target cell information to minimize target information loss; Additionally, to solve the problem of poor segmentation accuracy due to the blurred cell boundaries, the Multi-scale Transformer Attention module is embedded between encoder and decoder, improving the transfer of the boundary feature information and makes the segmented cell boundaries more accurate. Experimental results on MoNuSeg, GlaS and CoNSeP datasets demonstrate the network's superior accuracy.
Introduction

Pathologic cell images provide an important basis for the diagnosis, prognosis, and treatment of diseases. Currently, pathologists usually use stained pathological cell images as the "gold standard" for cancer diagnosis. Among them, the morphological characteristics of pathological cell nuclei are one of the main bases for pathological diagnosis, and an in-depth understanding of the morphological changes of cell nuclei in pathological cell images is of great significance for diagnosis and differentiation. By utilizing the automatic and precise segmentation of pathological cells by computer, it not only helps medical experts analyze changes in the morphology of cell nuclei more accurately, but also provides a more reliable basis for the diagnosis, prognosis, and therapeutic methods of cancer. Additionally, the technique can be seamlessly integrated with pathology image processing software, offering pathologists auxiliary tools to help them analyze and process pathology images more efficiently in a busy clinical environment. Thus, nucleus segmentation is a key basis for pathological cellular diagnosis and has important research value and significance in pathologic histology.

Currently, the methods of medical cell segmentation by computer are primarily categorized into traditional segmentation methods and deep learning-based segmentation methods. Traditional segmentation methods mainly include the threshold method, watershed method, region growing method, clustering method, morphological method, etc. However, traditional algorithms solve cell segmentation with a series of disadvantages such as complex and cumbersome preprocessing and postprocessing processes, difficult and long time to extract features, and lack of generalization, which makes it not ideal in terms of segmentation accuracy and efficiency. Convolution-based deep learning segmentation methods have the advantage of automatic feature extraction, can be trained end-to-end, and have better segmentation results than traditional methods.

Subsequently, various structures based on convolutional neural networks have been applied to image segmentation. One of the classic works is the Fully Convolutional Network (FCN), which can be further extended from image-level classification to pixel-level classification, thus allowing end-to-end model training and segmentation results. These structures include SegNet LinkNet, DeepLab, Enet, UNet, nnU-Net, MedNeXt, and others. Although they all achieve better results on classical segmentation datasets, they also have some shortcomings. For example, the high-level semantic information of the SegNet network is not well combined with the shallow image information, and the segmentation will produce more noise points and blurred edges in the image; LinkNet will miss the segmentation of small targets; DeepLab can fully learn global and local contextual information in the image. However the segmentation effect on small targets is not good, and at the same time it needs a large amount of labeled data for training in order to have better results; ENet segmented semantic image boundaries are blurred, mainly due to the lack of utilization of shallow structural information of the image, which makes segmentation accuracy can not meet the requirements; UNet is easy to cause information loss in the process of downsampling, and cannot accurately segment multi-targets; nnU-Net does not require manual parameter tuning, which reduces the influence of manual labor on the model. However, the model is prone to overfitting; MedNeXt introduces a large kernel convolution to maintain the richness of the feature information across the scales. However, it also results in a large amount of operating costs.

In the field of pathological cell segmentation, Song et al. proposed a multi-scale convolutional neural network and graph partitioning-based model to solve the segmentation of nucleus and cytoplasm in pathological images, which effectively reduces the computational complexity of the segmentation by using the super-pixel approach. However, the model based on the convolutional neural network can only extract some local features, which limits performance limited. BenTaieb et al. proposed the FCN model with multiple loss functions to solve pancreas segmentation in pathological cells and improve segmentation accuracy from the perspective of loss functions. However, the model requires certain class prior conditions and lacks consideration of global context, which leaves room for improvement in the model's segmentation performance. Chen et al. proposed a depth contour-aware model to solve gland instance segmentation, which performs well when facing cells with large appearance variations. However, the model performance is more general when facing the problem of small and dense nuclei in pathological cells. Zhou et al. proposed a contour-aware information aggregation model by adding an information fusion module between the encoder and decoder. This solved the problem that the model could not be learned due to incorrect labeling. However, due to the small size of pathological cells, it is difficult for the information fusion module to learn effective boundary information of the pathological cells, which results in poor segmentation performance. Lin et al. proposed a dual Transformer's encoder-decoder, which can extract the features from the perspective of between different scales of features and the long-distance feature information and thus improve the segmentation accuracy of the pathological cells. However, the model fails to fully utilize the underlying information of the pathological cells, which leads to a rough final segmentation result. The above deep learning-based methods have made great progress in pathology cell segmentation. However, the limitations of their algorithms make it difficult to better solve the problem of poor segmentation accuracy due to dense pathological cells, complex backgrounds, and blurred cell boundaries.

Therefore, in order to further improve the segmentation accuracy of the algorithm in pathological cell images, we propose a pathological cell segmentation method based on the multi-scale Transformer and multi-attention mechanism. Unlike existing methods that primarily focus on local feature extraction, our method introduces a Dense-CA module in the encoder part of a U-Net structure. This module improves feature extraction by adaptively focusing on target features, thereby reducing information loss during downsampling and improving the model's ability to distinguish between target nuclei and background. To further enhance boundary segmentation, we introduce a multi-scale Transformer attention (MSTA) module that bridges the encoder and decoder, utilizing Transformer-based feature fusion to extract nuclei boundary information from different scales. Furthermore, the inclusion of channel cross-attention helps mitigate overfitting and allows the model to learn more refined boundary information. This approach ensures that the two modules, Dense-CA and MSTA, work synergistically, with Dense-CA focusing on feature extraction and MSTA refining boundary precision.
The main contributions of this paper are summarized as follows:

(1)Aiming at the problem that the complex background and high density of pathological cell images make it difficult for the model to extract features, we design a Dense-CA module in the encoder process, which improves the model's ability to extract the target features in the encoder in order to reduce the model's loss of information in the downsampling. By adaptively emphasizing the relevant features, the Dense-CA module improves the model's ability to distinguish the target nuclei from the background, thereby significantly enhancing the segmentation accuracy of pathological cells;

(2) Aiming at the problem of poor boundary segmentation accuracy due to the blurring of pathological cell boundaries, we design a MSTA module, which fuses the features between the encoder and the decoder, and makes the model capable of extracting the nuclei boundary information more efficiently by re-combining the features of different scales with the multi-scale features on a single channel. Additionally, introduce a channel cross-attention mechanism to enhance feature fusion in the decoder to prevent model overfitting. As a result, the model achieves improved accuracy in segmentation of nuclei boundaries.
Related works
Traditional methods

Traditional pathology image segmentation methods usually rely on manually designed feature extraction and classification strategies. Common traditional methods include techniques based on threshold segmentation, edge detection, and region growing. These methods rely on preprocessing and manual adjustment of image features and usually achieve good results in simple pathology images. However, these methods tend to perform poorly when dealing with challenging pathology images with complex backgrounds, dense cellularity, and blurred cell boundaries because they lack effective global contextual information and modeling capabilities for complex image features. With the gradual increase in the complexity of medical images, the limitations of the traditional methods gradually become apparent, especially when facing the diversity and complexity of targets in pathology images, the accuracy and robustness significantly decrease.
Deep learning

With the rapid development of deep learning technology, especially the successful application of convolutional neural networks (CNNs) in various tasks, significant breakthroughs have been achieved in pathology image segmentation technology. In particular, the U-Net-based encoder-decoder architecture shows obvious advantages over other deep learning segmentation methods in terms of training sample requirements, memory occupation, segmentation accuracy, and computation time. Therefore, most pathology image segmentation methods are based on U-Net as the basic framework to improve the segmentation accuracy and efficiency. For example, H-DenseUNet combines the ideas of densely connected networks and U-Net to achieve effective aggregation for contextual feature information. UNet++ reduces semantic gap between the feature maps of the encoder and decoder sub-networks by using densely skip connection encoders and decoders between layers. FU-Net reduces semantic gaps between the feature maps of the encoder and decoder sub-networks by designing a dynamically weighted cross-entropy loss function to improve U-Net by weighting each pixel from images with poor prediction results to improve segmentation accuracy. ANU-Net redesigned the U-Net structure with nested dense jumps to integrate different levels of features for higher segmentation performance. Inspired by the above methods, dense joining fuses the features from top to bottom convolutional layers of the network, which alleviates the situation of gradient vanishing in the network, and at the same time, it can improve the reuse rate of the features under the condition of complex background features. At the same time, the proposed attention mechanism further enhances the capture of target features, the dense connection can reuse features and the channel attention does not cause excessive memory consumption compared with other attention. Therefore, in this paper, after considering the above advantages, we decided to introduce the combination of dense connectivity and dense channel attention into the encoder part, and further improve the encoder to improve the feature learning ability and reduce the information loss in the downsampling process.
Transformer

The local nature attributed to convolutional operations makes it difficult to capture global and remote semantic information using purely convolutional U-Net models, and this detailed spatial information can help the model to accurately segment complex pathological cell segmentation tasks. Inspired by a Transformer model proposed by Vaswani et al. in the field of Natural Language Processing, which would realize the dependencies between remote pixels through a self-attentive mechanism, the approach has achieved state-of-the-art performance in classification, target detection, and semantic segmentation tasks. Therefore, it has been continuously applied to the field of pathological image segmentation by researchers, such as Chen et al., who proposed the TransNet model, which provides a hierarchical CNN transformation structure that realizes the CNN to extract the low-level features and the Transformer to capture the global information and achieves better results in the tasks of multiorgan segmentation and cardiac segmentation. Cao et al. presented a model of a U-Net encoder-decoder structure combined with a Swin-Transformer block, which uses various windows to alleviate the computational burden of window shifting, realizes an effective reduction of the computational burden of interactions between windows, and proves that Transformer-based encoder-decoder network outperforms fully convolutional or combined Transformer-convolutional methods. Therefore, in this paper, after considering all the advantages mentioned above, we decided to replace the traditional jump connection part with a Transformer, and fully integrate the features of the encoder and decoder.
Method

In pathological cell images, due to the high density of pathological cell nuclei, complex background, and blurred cell boundaries, the segmentation method based on the common U-Net and Transformer as the basic architecture is difficult to extract the target features of pathological cells, and it is very easy to cause the phenomenon of mis-segmentation in the boundary segmentation, which makes the segmentation accuracy limited. To better adapt to pathological cell segmentation, we propose a method based on a multi-scale Transformer and multi-attention mechanism on the architecture of U-Net, and the overall framework of the algorithm model is shown in Fig. 1.
The pathological nuclei segmentation framework with multiscale Transformers and multi-attention.

The Dense-CA module, based on dense connectivity, innovatively incorporates a channel attention mechanism to enhance target feature weights and reduce memory usage, improving feature extraction. This design is particularly effective for pathological images with complex backgrounds and dense cell nuclei, where traditional methods struggle. By optimizing target feature weights, the Dense-CA module improves target-background separation and segmentation accuracy, and supports the application of a multi-scale Transformer cross-attention mechanism for further fusion of global and multi-scale information, enhancing overall model performance. To further boost boundary segmentation in complex cases, we combine Dense-CA with a multiscale Transformer attention (MSTA) module. MSTA fuses features at different scales with cross-self-attention, enabling better recognition of fuzzy cell boundaries. This combination strengthens boundary extraction in complex backgrounds, significantly enhancing segmentation accuracy, with Dense-CA focusing on feature extraction and MSTA on boundary precision.

Dense channel attention (Dense-CA) module

Pathology images, which have complex backgrounds and dense cell nuclei, often lose target features during U-Net downsampling, limiting segmentation accuracy. Adding network layers can deepen feature learning, but it requires a large number of parameters and complicates gradient training. Gao Huang et al. addressed this with dense connections, which concatenate each layer's output to subsequent layers, improving feature retention and minimizing information loss. Dense connections suit pathology tasks with limited data, while channel attention mechanisms enhance target focus by weighting essential channels. To address high-density nuclei and complex backgrounds, we propose a Dense-CA module, integrating dense connections and channel attention to stabilize downsampling and highlight target features.
Dense connectivity mechanism

A dense connection means that the input of each layer of the network is the concatenation of the outputs of all the preceding layers, and the output of each layer will be passed to all the following layers as input. Multiscale transformer attention (MSTA) module

Long-range global and multi-scale features are crucial for segmenting ambiguous boundaries in pathological cell images. However, classical U-Net, relying on convolution, captures mainly local features and lacks efficient global feature extraction. Inspired by Transformer's capability for long-range dependency capture, early models like TransUNet and Swin-UNet enhanced segmentation performance by adding a Transformer module for feature extraction or as an additional branch. These methods improved encoders and decoders but overlooked the skip connections, which merge features at various scales. Transformer integration into skip connections could further transfer global features, enhancing segmentation accuracy. However, improper use at multiple scales can lead to overfitting, posing a challenge in effectively leveraging Transformer features. Recent studies suggest that introducing convolution into self-attention improves localization, allowing multi-scale feature fusion. This paper proposes a multiscale Transformer attention (MSTA) module, replacing traditional skip connections with a multiscale channel-crossing Transformer to bridge encoder and decoder features. The MSTA module, composed of a multi-scale channel-crossing Transformer and channel-crossing attention, enhances feature fusion, addressing segmentation difficulties caused by blurred cell boundaries.

Experiments and results
Datasets

To validate the effectiveness of the method proposed in this paper, it was evaluated on the histopathology image public dataset MoNuSeg, the glandular dataset GlaS, and the colorectal dataset CoNSeP. The MoNuSeg dataset, from the 2018 MICCAI (Medical Image Computing and Computer Assisted Intervention) challenge, consists of images captured by The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) from Whole Slide Images (WSIs). Each image has a size of 10001000 pixels and contains multi-organ cell nuclei data from eight organs: breast, liver, kidney, colon, and stomach. For this experiment, 30 images were used for training and 14 images for testing. The GlaS dataset, sourced from the 2015 MICCAI Gland Segmentation Challenge, focuses on gland segmentation in colorectal tissue. The images in this dataset have a maximum size of 552775 pixels, and the main anatomical region is the colorectum. In this experiment, 85 images were used for training and 80 images for testing. The CoNSeP dataset is derived from 16 colorectal adenocarcinoma (CRA) WSIs, each corresponding to a unique patient. These WSIs were scanned using an Omnyx VL120 scanner at the Department of Pathology, University Hospitals Coventry and Warwickshire, UK. Each image is 10001000 pixels in size. For this experiment, 20 images were used for training and 14 images for testing.
Experimental settings

The computing platform chosen for this experiment is the Pytorch deep learning framework, the programming language is Python 3.9, and the hardware of the graphics processing unit (GPU) is NVIDIA RTX 3060. In the MoNuSeg and CoNSeP datasets, cell regions are typically small and densely packed, making certain data augmentation operations necessary to mitigate overfitting. Given the large size and high information density of pathological cell images, overfitting can become more prominent, especially with smaller datasets. To address this, a variety of data augmentation techniques are applied to the pathology images, including horizontal flip, vertical flip, and random rotation. Specifically, the horizontal flip mirrors the image by , and the vertical flip further increases data diversity by flipping the image  vertically. The random rotation operation randomly selects an angle between  and  to rotate the image, filling any missing parts with zero padding. These augmentation techniques effectively increase the diversity of training data, thereby enhancing the model's robustness and its ability to adapt to geometric changes such as rotation and flipping. Consequently, the generalization capability of the model is further strengthened.

The following hyperparameters were used in this experiment: the batch size is set to 4, the learning rate is 1e-3, and the model is trained for 2000 epochs. The Adam optimizer was used with the initial learning rate of 0.001. The network is trained using a combination of cross-entropy loss and dice loss as the loss function. To make the results on the dataset more convincing, three 5-fold cross-validations (15 CVs in total) were performed to obtain the average result as the final result.
Evaluation metrics

In order to realize the quantitative analysis of the network on the cell nucleus segmentation results, this paper adopts two performance indexes, Dice similarity coefficient (Dice) and intersection over union (IOU), as the evaluation criteria. Among them, true positives (TP) represent actual nuclei, and the segmentation results are predicted to be nuclei as well. False positives (FP) represent the actual background and the segmentation result is predicted to be the nucleus. True Negative (TN) represents the actual background, and the segmentation result is predicted to be the background. False Negative (FN): represents the actual nucleus and the segmentation result is predicted to be the background.

(1) Dice is used to measure the overlap between the segmentation result and the labeled image, with a value between 0 and 1. The larger the value, the better the segmentation effect. The calculation formula is shown in Equation (17).(2) IOU is a commonly used evaluation criterion in semantic segmentation, it is the ratio of the intersection of predicted result (PR) and real label (ground truth, GT) and their concatenation, and the output result is used as the accuracy of medical image segmentation, and the optimal state value is 1, and the closer to 1 means that the segmentation result is the more similar to the label, and the formula of IOU is shown in Equation (18).

passages.text: In order to fully explore and analyze the effectiveness of the proposed modules in this paper for the task of pathology image segmentation, ablation experiments were conducted on the Dense-CA and MSTA modules to compare the model segmentation performance before and after the improvement. In the first experiment, the U-Net is alone applied for pathological nuclei segmentation. The second experiment was "U-Net with Dense-CA". The third experiment was "U-Net with MSTA". The fourth experiment was "U-Net with Dense-CA+ MSTA". The results of the ablation experiments are shown in Table 1.

From the experimental results in Table 1, it can be seen that, on the one hand, the transfer ability of the features after adding the Dense-CA module is improved, making the target features more obvious and thus the network model's ability to capture the cellular targets, the Dice values on the two datasets of MoNuSeg, GlaS and CoNSeP are improved compared to 76.45, 89.45 and 78.26 of the baseline network U-Net, respectively, to 78.77, 91.76 and 79.36. On the other hand, in adding the MSTA module, the channel-crossing Transformer mechanism in this module replaces the original jump connection to make the model more sensitive to the boundary information, and the channel-crossing attention further reduces the risk of overfitting in the model, and the Dice values are improved by 2.43, 2.04 and 1.1 respectively. Finally, after adding the Dense-CA and MSTA modules, the Dice value finally reaches 80.44, 92.44 and 79.36, and it can be concluded that the effective fit between the two modules, under the premise of making the target features obvious, the ability to extract the boundary information of the target is also improved accordingly, which makes the boundary of the segmentation results clearer, and then improves the segmentation accuracy of the whole model for pathological cells.

Visualization of ablation experiment results. The first and second rows are the MoNuSeg dataset, the third and fourth rows are the GlaS dataset, and the fifth row is the CoNSeP dataset. (a) Original image, (b) Ground Truth, (c) Baseline(U-Net), (d) Baseline+Dense-CA, (e) Baseline+MSTA, (f) ours.

Through the analysis of Fig. 4, it is evident that the traditional U-Net architecture faces limitations in accurately segmenting complex pathological cells, especially when dealing with high-density nuclei, complex backgrounds, and blurred boundaries. As seen in the fourth column of Fig. 4, the introduction of the Dense-CA module enhances the extraction of pathological cell features and improves localization of cell nuclei, yet it still struggles to achieve precise segmentation of cell boundaries. In contrast, the addition of the MSTA module, as shown in the fifth column, significantly enhances boundary segmentation accuracy, particularly for densely packed or large nuclei. However, the second row of Fig. 4 highlights a trade-off: while the MSTA module alone effectively reduces noise, it may also introduce missegmentation in larger regions. By integrating both the Dense-CA and MSTA modules in our approach, we leverage the Dense-CA module during encoding to suppress noise while allowing the MSTA module to enhance multiscale feature learning. This combined approach enables the model to be more sensitive to boundary details and increases the segmentation accuracy of pathological cells. The overall results show a high similarity to the ground truth labels, demonstrating the method's effectiveness in addressing the complex requirements of pathological cell image segmentation.

This indicates that the downsampling and maximum pooling operations in the encoder part do cause the loss of target information, which makes it difficult for the model to extract the target features in the pathology cell images and prevent accurate segmentation. Compared with the other four models, the overall results of the segmentation of the model in this paper are closer to the true value map, which indicates that the Dense-CA module can improve the reuse rate of the improved features and inhibit the occurrence of the phenomenon of gradient disappearance, and at the same time, the addition of channel attention also makes the target features more obvious, which in turn makes the model to extract more information about the target features. Observing the detailed segmentation results in Fig. 6, we find that the segmentation results of Swin-Unet and AttNet are not fine enough and there are a lot of mis-segmentation phenomena, which indicates that the use of the Transformer and the attention mechanism in the encoder and decoder part can not be effectively segmented on the image boundary, which is very prone to cause the phenomenon of mis-segmentation. From the figure, it can be seen that the model in this paper has a finer segmentation profile compared with other models, indicating that the MSTA module, which can make full use of the features of different scales, further enhances the boundary features of the pathological cells, and at the same time introduces the channel cross-attention mechanism to prevent the model from overfitting, which makes the model very sensitive to the boundary information of the cells. It can be seen that the method in this paper can effectively improve the segmentation accuracy of pathological cell images.

This improvement is attributed to the inherent limitations of U-Net-based models in feature extraction, particularly when dealing with pathology cell images that have a large number of background features, high nucleus density, and fuzzy boundaries. In contrast, the method presented here enhances the U-Net network by introducing a multi-scale Transformer and multi-attention mechanism. Compared with the basic U-Net, the Dice values are improved by 3.99, 2.99 and 1.1 in the three datasets, respectively. Conclusion and discussions

Aiming at the problems of the fuzzy boundary of pathological cells, high density of cell nuclei, and complex background. In this paper, we propose a multi-scale Transformer and multi-attention mechanism segmentation method with encoder-decoder as the basic framework. In order to solve the problem of high cell nucleus density and complex background that makes it difficult for the model to extract the features, we propose the Dense-CA module in the encoder part to repeat the learning of the information featured in the encoder and the semantic information of the target features is enhanced by the weights of the target features strengthened by the channel attention so that the model can effectively capture the target features; In order to solve the problem of poor boundary segmentation accuracy due to the blurring of pathological cell boundaries, we propose the MSTA module to connect the multiscale features in the encoder and decoder, to extract the features of each layer and to fully fuse the features of each channel, and then to further fuse them with the feature information of each layer of the decoder through the channel cross-attention, to make it more sensitive to the boundary information of the cells. The model is compared with the algorithm based on the U-Net model and state-of-the-art algorithms, and experiments are conducted on the multi-organ dataset MoNuSeg dataset, the gland dataset GlaS dataset and the colorectal dataset CoNSeP. The experimental results show that without any pre-training, the Dice coefficient of segmentation accuracy of the method based on the multi-scale Transformer and multi-attention Mechanism for pathology images reaches 80.44, 92.44 and 79.36 respectively, and the model evaluation indexes are better than other algorithms.
FLOPs and total parameters for different models.

The computational complexity and efficiency results in Fig. 7 show that the proposed method in this paper is significantly different from existing algorithms. Due to the introduction of the Dense-CA module, the number of parameters in this paper's method reaches 122 million, which is significantly higher compared to models such as U-Net (14.75 million), UCTransNet (66.43 million) and DeepLabv3 (62.23 million). Moreover, the FLOPs of our model (42.26 GFLOPs) are also higher than those of U-Net (25.21 GFLOPs) and UCTransNet (32.98 GFLOPs), but lower than those of UNet2Plus (152.85 GFLOPs) and UNet3Plus (152.93 GFLOPs). Although the model can run on a server, its computational complexity and resource consumption could pose challenges, especially for real-time applications in clinical settings. To address this, future research should focus on developing more efficient feature extraction methods, such as model pruning to remove redundant parameters and reduce complexity, or knowledge distillation to transfer the knowledge from a large model to a smaller one without compromising performance. These approaches can help improve inference speed and reduce storage requirements, particularly in resource-constrained environments.

Additionally, while various data augmentation techniques and pre-training strategies were applied to the MoNuSeg and CoNSeP datasets, overfitting remains a significant issue, suggesting that the model's performance could still be improved with larger and more diverse datasets. Advanced data augmentation techniques, including more aggressive transformations, are needed to further enhance the model's robustness. Moreover, instance segmentation remains a challenging task due to overlapping and adhesion of cells in medical images. Future work should explore further advancements in cell nucleus instance segmentation, potentially leveraging Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) to improve segmentation accuracy and assist in disease diagnosis.

passages.text: Dietary vitamin intake and its association with hypertension (HPT) among Malaysian adults

This study aims to investigate the association between dietary vitamin (A, B6, B9, B12, C, E, and K) intake and hypertension (HPT) among Malaysian adult population. This is a cross-sectional analysis of baseline data from a population-based cohort of 10,031 participants from the Malaysia arm of the Prospective Urban and Rural Epidemiology (PURE) study. Participants were classified as having HPT if they reported a diagnosis of high blood pressure (systolic blood pressure (SBP)/diastolic blood pressure (DBP) > 140/90). Participants' usual dietary intake was assessed using a validated food frequency questionnaire. Vitamin (A, B6, B9, B12, C, E, and K) intake was calculated using nutrient databases. The Mann-Whitney U test was used to assess differences in vitamin intake between the HPT groups. This study found that the prevalence of HPT among 10,031 respondents was 43.5%. The overall dietary intake of vitamins A and C was adequate, but the intake of vitamins B6, B9, B12, E, and K was inadequate compared to Malaysia's Recommended Nutrient Intakes (RNI). The intake of vitamins A, B6, B9, B12, E, and K was significantly lower among patients with HPT compared to those without HPT (p-value < 0.001). This study found that the Malaysian adult population is not receiving sufficient intake of vitamins B6, B9, B12, E, and K from their diet. Improving vitamin intake can be achieved through nutrition education, a diet that includes a variety of healthy foods, and food fortification and supplementation.

passages.text: Introduction

Vitamins perform a variety of roles in the body, such as facilitating the production of enzymes, hormones and other essential compounds for normal growth and development. The National Coordinating Committee on Food and Nutrition of the Malaysia Ministry of Health has established detailed Recommended Nutrient Intakes (RNI) as the standard for determining the recommended vitamin intake. Previous research in Malaysia has revealed that while the adult population's intake of vitamins A and C is sufficient, their intake of vitamins E, B9, B12, and K falls short of the RNI.

annotations.text: vitamins E, B9, B12, and K

passages.text: Despite the fact that vitamins are required only in minimal quantities, their impact on overall health is crucial. A deficiency in any one vitamin can lead to visible and serious health conditions. Vitamin deficiencies can also cause reductions in energy levels, cognitive function, and overall capacity, leading to decreased work productivity and increased susceptibility to other diseases and health problems. HPT is a health condition that can be affected by vitamin deficiency. Previous research has shown a positive association between HPT and vitamin deficiency. This relationship is due to the role of vitamins in regulating blood pressure (BP) through their effects on diuretics, the sympathetic nervous system (SNS), vascular modulators, and calcium channel blockers (CCBs). Given the inadequate vitamin intake among the Malaysian population and the vital role these nutrients play in controlling HPT, this study aims to investigate the association between dietary vitamin intake and HPT in the Malaysian adult population.
Methodology
Study design and population

The PURE study is a large-scale international effort to investigate the incidence, mortality and risk factors associated with non-communicable diseases among individuals living in urban and rural communities across 27 countries, including Malaysia. The study, led by the Population Health Research Institute (PHRI) in Hamilton, Ontario, Canada, initiated data collection in 2007 and follow-up is projected to continue until 2030. In Malaysia, data collection is carried out jointly by the Universiti Kebangsaan Malaysia (UKM) and the Universiti Teknologi MARA (UiTM). The PURE enrolled 15,792 Malaysian individuals aged 35 to 70 in the baseline phase. The study design has been described previously.

In brief, community leaders from selected urban and rural areas were approached, and their permission was obtained to set up health screening and promotion booths in the communities' assembly halls. Interested and eligible participants were briefed about the study during these activities. After providing written informed consent, participants provided their medical histories and underwent basic physical examinations. Home visits were arranged to further engage with family members living in the same household, who were also invited to participate in the study. To ensure the feasibility of long-term follow-up, only household members intending to reside in the same household for at least four more years were included.
Measurements

Participants were classified as part of the HPT group if they reported a previous diagnosis of HPT or recorded high blood pressure (systolic blood pressure (SBP)/diastolic blood pressure (DBP) > 140/90) during physical examination. An automatic Omron blood pressure monitor (model HEM-7111) was used to measure participants' resting blood pressure.

Participants' usual dietary intake was assessed using a validated food frequency questionnaire (FFQ). Participants were asked how often they consumed various food items over the past year, with options ranging from never to more than six times per day. Standard serving sizes (e.g., one egg, one tablespoon and one cup) were assigned to each food item. Then, dietary vitamin (A, B6, B9, B12, C, E, and K) intake was calculated based on the Malaysian and US Department of Agriculture food composition databases, with reference to nutrient databases containing recipes of mixed dishes.

passages.text: Demographic, personal and family medical history data were extracted from the validated PURE questionnaire, and physical activity levels were assessed using the International Physical Activity Questionnaire (IPAQ). Demographic characteristics included age (<= 40 or > 40), gender (male or female), education level (low or high), socio-economic status (low or middle-high), employment status (yes or no), and marital status (currently married or currently unmarried). Residency area (urban or rural) was determined based on local government-gazetted areas, with rural defined as areas with less than 150 residents per square kilometer.

Height and weight were measured using a portable stature meter and the TANITA (BC-558 Ironman ) segmental body composition analyzer, respectively. Body Mass Index (BMI) was calculated by dividing weight (in kilograms) by height (in meters) squared. A BMI of < 25 kg/m2 was categorized as normal, and a BMI of >= 25 kg/m2 as overweight-obese. Physical activity level was considered low if it was < 600 Metabolic Equivalent (MET) min/week and high if it was >= 600 MET min/week.
Statistical analysis

The data were analyzed using SPSS version 26. A chi-square test was used to assess differences among the HPT group according to the following variables: age, gender, residency, education level, socio-economic status (SES), employment status, marital status, BMI, physical activity, co-morbidity, and family history of HPT and diabetes mellitus (DM). The Mann-Whitney U test was then used to assess differences in vitamin intake between the HPT groups. Results were reported as frequencies, percentages, medians, and interquartile ranges (IQR). A p-value of < 0.05 was considered statistically significant.
Results

Of the 15,792 recruited participants, 10,031 completed the medical history assessment of HPT and FFQ. The prevalence of HPT among these 10,031 respondents from this study was 43.5% (n = 4365). The socio-demographic characteristics of this study population are summarized in Table 1. HPT was more prevalent among those over 40 years old (48.0%), residing in rural areas (48.0%), with low education (54.2%), lower socio-economic status (48.2%), currently unmarried (48.2%), overweight-obese BMI (46.6%), with co-morbidity of DM (68.4%), and with a family history of HPT (48.7%).

The comparison of vitamin intake among the Malaysian adult population with RNI is summarized in Table 2. Their overall dietary intake of vitamins A and C was found to be adequate, but not for vitamins B6, B9, B12, E, and K, compared to the RNI. The median vitamin A intake was 1164.0 (IQR: 644.2-1610.2) microg/day, approximately double the RNI (600 microg/day). Similarly, the median vitamin C intake was 109.3 (IQR: 64.4-166.7) mg/day, compared to the recommended 70 mg/day. However, intake of vitamin B-complex (B6, B9, and B12) was found to be inadequate, with median intake levels of 0.2 (0.1-0.4) mg/day, 36.7 (IQR: 20.4-66.5) microg/day, and 1.3 (IQR: 0.6-2.4) microg/day, respectively, compared to the RNI (1.3-1.7 mg/day, 400 microg/day and 4.0 microg/day). The same trend was observed for dietary intake of vitamins E and K (1.6 (IQR: 0.8-3.0) mg/day and 18.2 (IQR: 5.1-36.7) microg/day, respectively) compared to the RNI (7.5-10 mg/day and 55-65 microg/day). Additionally, dietary intake of vitamins A (median: 1087.4, IQR: 600.7-1564.1 microg/day), B6 (median: 0.2, IQR: 0.1-0.4 mg/day), B9 (median: 34.2, IQR: 19.5-59.9 microg/day), B12 (median: 1.2, IQR: 0.5-2.4 microg/day), E (median: 1.4, IQR: 0.6-2.9 mg/day), and K (median: 15.6, IQR: 3.9-35.9 microg/day) among HPT patients was significantly lower compared to those without HPT vitamin A (median: 1216.1, IQR: 690.9-1632.3 microg/day), B6 (median: 0.3, IQR: 0.1-0.5 mg/day), B9 (median: 38.4, IQR: 21.6-70.6 microg/day), B12 (median: 1.5, IQR: 0.7-2.8 microg/day), E (median: 1.8, IQR: 0.9-3.5 mg/day), and K (median: 19.9, IQR: 6.4-47.5 microg/day) with p-value < 0.001).

Discussion

The prevalence of HPT in this study was found to be 43.5%, which is higher than rates reported in the National Health and Morbidity Survey (NHMS) in 2011 (32.6%), 2015 (30.3%) and 2019 (30.0%). This study showed that HPT was more prevalent among those aged over 40 years old. This is likely due to the natural stiffening of blood vessels that occurs as people age. The population of HPT patients were found to be more prone in rural areas, and with low education and socio-economic status. Previous research has linked these factors to low health literacy, which can impede the ability to make informed health decisions. This is further compounded by limited access to healthy lifestyles due to financial constraints. Additionally, this study found that HPT was more prevalent among those with a BMI in the range of overweight-obese. This aligns with epidemiological evidence strongly suggesting an association between increased BMI and HPT. Furthermore, HPT was found to be more common in those with co-morbid DM and a family history of HPT. Previous research has demonstrated a positive association between blood glucose abnormalities and BP, with DM increasing the risk of stage 1 HPT by nearly 50%. Furthermore, genetic factors such as high sodium-lithium counter-transport, elevated uric acid levels, high fasting plasma insulin concentrations, fat pattern index, and BMI can contribute to the relationship between HPT and family history.

The overall dietary vitamin intake among the study population was insufficient compared to the recommended levels set by the Malaysian RNI, with the exception of vitamins A and C. These results align with previous studies conducted in Malaysia, which have also reported satisfactory dietary intake of vitamins A and C among the adult population. However, Lee and Muda reported that Malaysian adults have an insufficient dietary intake of vitamins B9, B12, E, and K compared to the RNI. This may be due to the low consumption of vegetables and dairy products in the Malaysian diet. Meanwhile, a US study has reported that dietary intake of vitamins B6, B9, B12, and K, but not vitamin E, was adequate among US adults. Low intake of vitamins C, B6, B9, B12, E, and K have been linked to an increased risk of HPT. Furthermore, this study found that HPT patients in Malaysia had significantly lower intake of vitamins A, B6, B9, B12, E, and K compared to those without HPT (Table 2).

passages.text: The primary function of vitamin A in HPT is to improve impaired endothelial function. This study found that HPT patients had a lower dietary intake of vitamin A compared to those without HPT, despite overall intake being sufficient according to the RNI. However, other studies have found that HPT patients have higher levels of retinol-binding protein 4 (RBP4), the main extracellular transport protein of vitamin A, compared to those without HPT. These findings suggest increased serum vitamin A in HPT patients may be due to impaired kidney function, leading to enhanced retention of the vitamin A-RBP4-prealbumin complex.

Previous studies have shown that low levels of vitamin B-complex (B6, B9 and B12) are associated with HPT. Vitamin B6 deficiency reduce the production of neurotransmitters serotonin and GABA, which can result in decreased phospholipids in the brain and changes in Ca2+ transport and metabolism. This can ultimately lead to increased BP. Vitamin B6 has also been reported to increase diuretic activity by regulating the SNS, improving glutathione production, and reducing inflammation, thus indirectly lowering BP. The potential antihypertensive effect of vitamins B9 and B12 may be due to a reduction in blood homocysteine concentrations through the demethylation of homocysteine to methionine. This can have a positive impact on regulating BP. According to Tamura et al., homocysteine has been linked to oxidative stress, endothelial dysfunction, inflammation, and decreased bioavailability of endothelium-derived nitric oxide, resulting in increased BP.

A study by Emami et al. discovered that supplementing with vitamin E improved SBP in HPT patients, but did not affect their DBP. According to Chiu et al., vitamin E has a modest hypotensive effect by increasing the production of nitric oxide (vasodilation) and prostaglandins I/E, which can reduce arterial stiffness and improve vascular endothelial function. Vitamin E also possesses natriuretic activity (diuretic) by inhibiting the 70PS K and Ca channels in the ascending limbs of the loops of Henle, thereby regulating BP. Additionally, its antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties may improve vascular function and lower BP.

Low vitamin K intake is associated with higher BP and an increased risk of HPT. Vitamin K plays a role in vascular calcification by acting as a cofactor in the carboxylation, or activation, of matrix Gla protein (MGP), a calcification inhibitor. Vitamin K deficiency, induced by vitamin K antagonists, can lead to under-carboxylated MGP and increased vascular calcification. Additionally, low expression or inactivation of vitamin K-dependent proteins can cause vascular stiffness, increasing BP and HPT risk.

This study has several limitations. Firstly, as it is a cross-sectional study, it cannot establish a causal relationship between dietary vitamin intake and HPT. Another limitation is that the dietary recall method used may not accurately reflect the actual intake of vitamins. Thus, we only included data with plausible energy intake in the range of 500 to 5000 Kcal in this study. To confirm the causal relationship between dietary vitamin intake and HPT, further studies using a prospective design and measuring vitamin levels in the body are needed. This current study focused on the direct association between vitamin intake and HPT status, without considering potential confounders such as socioeconomic status and education level that could influence the vitamin intake and HPT status. The lack of adjustment of potential confounders to provide a more comprehensive analysis may limit the depth of our conclusion. The future research should explore these associations comprehensively.

Despite these limitations, the findings of this study highlight significant implications for public health and clinical practice regarding HPT management in Malaysia. The high prevalence of HPT, particularly among individuals over 40 years of age and those with lower socio-economic status and education levels, underscores the need for targeted interventions that address these vulnerable populations. The insufficient dietary intake of essential vitamins, particularly B6, B9, B12, E, and K, suggests that nutritional deficiencies may exacerbate HPT and its related complications. This indicates a critical need for public health initiatives that not only promote nutritional education but also improve access to nutrient-dense foods for the vulnerable population. Furthermore, the association between low vitamin intake and HPT emphasizes the importance of integrating dietary assessments into routine healthcare for hypertensive patients. Clinicians should consider nutritional status as a vital component of HPT management, encouraging dietary modifications and, where appropriate, supplementation to enhance overall health outcomes. These findings also suggest that future research should explore the potential benefits of targeted nutritional interventions in managing HPT and its comorbidities, particularly in populations identified as high-risk.

passages.text: Conclusion

This study found that the dietary intake of vitamins by Malaysian adults was sufficient for vitamins A and C, but inadequate for vitamins B6, B9, B12, E, and K compared to the RNI. Furthermore, this study found HPT patients had significantly lower intake levels vitamins A, B6, B9, B12, E, and K compared to their counterparts. Vitamins play an important role in regulating BP through mechanisms such as diuretics, SNS and vascular modulation, and calcium channel blockers (CCB). Therefore, an adequate and balanced intake of vitamins is crucial for controlling BP and reducing risk of HPT. This can be achieved through education on healthy nutrition, consuming a balanced diet, and using food fortification and supplementation. For those with HPT, it is also important to take medication in addition to ensuring adequate vitamin intake, as the condition can affect the metabolism of these nutrients in human body.

passages.text: Effects of steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome serum on AA pathway in podocytes cultured in 3D in vitro glomerular model

Steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome (SRNS) is the most severe form of nephrotic syndrome, with genetic or unidentified immunological origins and rapidly progressing to the need for kidney replacement therapy. Lipotoxicity can affect podocytes inducing kidney damage. In this study, we evaluate the effects of SRNS serum on podocyte functionality and lipid metabolism. A three-dimensional (3D) dynamic in vitro glomerulus was incubated with serum from multi-drug resistant (MDR) and genetic SRNS or healthy controls. The glomerular filtration barrier (GFB) integrity, podocyte viability, and fatty acids (FAs) composition were evaluated by serum albumin permeability estimation, cytofluorimetric analysis and gas chromatography, respectively. Expression of slit diaphragm molecules and FA-related enzymes was analyzed by immunofluorescence and PCR. Serum from SRNS patients induced cell granularity, increased GFB permeability, and disrupted slit diaphragm protein structure. The podocyte damage was most severe when MDR serum was administered compared to the serum of genetic-SRNS. This was associated with a significant upregulation of the transcripts coding for nephrin, synaptopodin, and CD2AP. An alteration of fatty acid profile in MDR-treated podocytes was observed, with increased monounsaturated FAs following the decrease of saturated FAs. The exposure of cultured podocytes to MDR- and genetic-SRNS serum induced disruption of arachidonic acid (AA) synthesis pathway, with different intermediate players involved. This study highlights the detrimental effects of serum from SRNS patients on podocyte function and the association of AA synthesis pathway with the podocyte damage.
Supplementary Information
The online version contains supplementary material available at 10.1038/s41598-025-95216-2.
Introduction

Idiopathic nephrotic syndrome (INS) is characterized by the presence of proteinuria, edema, and hyperlipemia. In childhood-onset INS, 10-15% of patients are steroid-resistant (SRNS), as they do not achieve remission with the initial treatment with steroids. Around 50% of them, unresponsive to second-line therapies, are classified as multi-drug resistant SRNS (MDR), the most severe form of the disease. Only in 1/3 of patients, a pathogenic variant of genes coding for structural proteins of the glomerular filtration barrier (GFB) has been identified (monogenic SRNS), while in the remaining cases, a yet unidentified immunological cause is thought to be involved. Both MDR and genetic SRNS are associated with poor kidney survival.

INS is characterized by the leakage of proteins as well as lipids into the urine and a concomitant increase of blood-free fatty acids. Leaked lipids mainly accumulate in the proximal tubules, inducing tubular damage and fibrosis. Excessive lipid uptake in podocytes can activate an oxidative stress response, inducing cell loss, which results in glomerular damage and proteinuria. Although lipid metabolism in the kidney seems to be a crucial issue, the link between podocyte lipotoxicity and INS is missing. Among fatty acids (FAs), arachidonic acid (AA) directly regulates podocyte integrity, by promoting slit diaphragm and cytoskeleton changes, mitochondrial fission, and cell apoptosis.AA has also been described to induce TGFbeta-mediated fibrosis in mesangial cells by activating inflammatory and pro-fibrotic genes, which are crucial in the progression of chronic kidney disease.

The pathophysiology of membranous nephropathy (MN) was shown to be related to AA metabolism by whole genome studies on human renal tissuesand through the analysis of AA metabolism-related enzymes in MN mouse models.
We recently reported the presence of elevated levels of AA in the blood of INS children at different clinical INS stages, supporting its role as a sensor of a persistent inflammatory milieu.

In this study, we used a three-dimensional (3D) dynamic glomerular model to investigate the lipotoxic alterations in human podocytes treated with serum from different forms of SRNS. The direct effects on podocyte cell viability, cytoskeleton organization, and slit diaphragm structure, were evaluated. The FA composition of podocytes cultured in the nephrotic syndrome-induced kidney model was also assessed.
Materials and methods
Patients and sample collection

This study was conducted according to the principles expressed in the Declaration of Helsinki. Approve to the study was obtained by the IRCCS Ca' Granda Institutional Review Board (ID 2633, INSiDe protocol). An informed consensus was obtained for all the participants enrolled in the study. Multi-drug resistant SRNS (MDR-SRNS, N = 5) and monogenic SRNS (MONO-SRNS, N = 5) patients were recruited during the active phase of the pathology in the Paediatric Nephrology, Dialysis and Renal Transplant Unit (Fondazione Ca' Granda IRCCS Ospedale Maggiore Policlinico, Milan). MDR-SRNS were defined as INS patients not achieving partial remission after at least 2 different lines of therapy other than steroids; monogenic SRNS forms were defined as patients non-responsive to immunosuppressive treatments and harboring a pathogenetic mutation in genes coding for components of GFB. The list of mutations was reported in Supplementary Table 1. Clinical data of SRNS patients were reported in Table 1. Furthermore, a group of healthy volunteers (N = 7) were also recruited as control group. The exclusion criteria for this group included fever, inherited, or acquired immune disorders, and the use of immunosuppressants. Serum samples were obtained by centrifuging whole blood at 3000 g for 20 minutes (min). Before each experiment, sera were diluted to 2% or 10% with either Dulbecco's modified Eagle's medium High Glucose (DMEM HG, Euroclone S.p.A., Pero MI, Italy) or EndoGROLS basal Culture Media (Merck Millipore, Burlington, Massachusetts, USA).
